utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with two administrative matters first. First of all, this afternoon we, because of the heat in here, we shall move to courtroom II and have the afternoon's hearings there. Secondly, tomorrow we have to adjourn at 12.00. There's a Status Conference in another case which two of our number have to attend. So in order to get more time in, unless it's inconvenient to anybody, we'll start at 9.00, sit from 9.00 to 12.00, perhaps have a slightly shorter break. Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. Yesterday I was criticised by the Prosecution relative to my cross-examination of Dr. Donia and an excerpt from Colonel Stewart's testimony, and that was read into the record. I suggest that the reading by Mr. Nice yesterday was out of context. The pages prior to and after the quote are important, and I'll leave it for the Court to decide, because I have pages 23826 through 23829, and you can see for yourself whether or not the context of which my question and the answer were appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you would like to hand those in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I might say that in relation to these sort of disputes between the parties, that I regard some of it as forensic. It's not the questions which matters, it's the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the question of timetable, I'm not going to pick up with Payam Akhavan, because Colonel Watters, who has been here twice before, is a witness whose examination in chief I hope will last less than half a day. I'm told by the Defence they require a day for him, but it may well be, as with some of their other forecasts, the forecasts will be longer than the reality, and it's really quite desirable that he should be concluded, this being his third visit, by tomorrow, if at all possible. He certainly can't be here next week for reason of other commitments. He is a colonel. His last deployment was to Northern Ireland, and for that reason I'm not going to ask him his present whereabouts. But obscuring his present whereabouts relates to that assignment and not to any anxiety about what happened in the former Yugoslavia. Because of the temperature of the court yesterday, I told him that it would be sensible for him not to turn up in uniform but to wear civilian clothes, and that's why he will appear dressed as he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness in. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm sorry, Your Honours. Just one word. Will you please bear in mind, even though you said that we would be discussing it on Thursday, but still would you like just to note down that the summary we received from the Prosecution regarding witness Bryan Watters is the third or the fourth that we're getting 30 or 40 minutes before the hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as that's concerned, the arrangement was, I thought, to be that the summary should be handed over, if possible, before the adjournment, the night before, so that the Defence would have a chance to look at it. If what is contained in the summary is merely what's in previous statements, then it seems there's less cause for complaint, but of course were there to be new matter, that would be a more substantial matter of complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as the Chamber will recall, this is an innovation designed to assist. It's outside the Rules. It's a voluntarily supplied document. My practice has been to provide it as early as possible. In nearly all cases, it is a reflection of material that the Defence have had in the form of statements or prior testimony. Whenever I can provide them the night before or even earlier, I do so. But in order that witnesses may not be inconvenienced too much, it's frequently the case that they only come in the day before they give testimony, and therefore the documents can't be prepared earlier. This was such a one. But I'm, in all cases, doing my best to ensure they are prepared as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that regard, since this is an experiment, some of the Prosecution's summaries have parentheses and where you can find the statements or the source, others do not. Of course, there's no formal rule. It would certainly be helpful to follow the current format, which is chapter and verse being cited, so new matter would pop right up for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That seems sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I'm doing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have the witness, please. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Bryan Shaun Charles Watters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A professional soldier in the British army for over 25 years, deputy commander of the 1st Cheshire Battle Corps during its deployment in Bosnia in 1993. Since then, have you been the lieutenant colonel in command of the 1st Cheshires, an appointment you relinquished at the beginning of this year, you remaining in the army as a professional soldier with a career ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On deployment in February of 1993, was your first task to familiarise yourself with the difficult military situation facing the warring factions, and in the course of that exercise, did you meet a number of key personalities in the military and political arena in Central Bosnia, particularly in Vitez, Kiseljak, Travnik and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the British Battalion's operation known as Grapple?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Operation Grapple 1, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was its formal objective or perhaps first objective to facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid throughout the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've put in the summary and, in inverted commas, the phrase "implied task". Can you just explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Our mission was to facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid throughout our area of responsibility. Within our doctrine in the British army and within the mission statements, there are tasks that are implied, and the tasks that were implied were to achieve the mission statement, we had to undertake various military tasks, and those tasks we would describe as implied tasks; for example, to stop fighting, to stop the loss of life, to stop ethnic cleansing, and anything we saw that prejudiced our ability to save life, which was the end state, if you like, or the ultimate implied task of our mission statement. The reason we were facilitating humanitarian aid was to save life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By application of this motion or doctrine or whatever it may be of implied task, did the range of functions performed by the British Battalion mirror and match the functions performed by other battalions, to your knowledge, or was it greater or lesser?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: By and large we all had the same task. We did it in our own way, and that largely depended on the capability or combat power that each of the battalions in the United Nations force had. By virtue of being an armoured infantry battalion, with our Warrior fighting vehicle, we had considerable combat power which others didn't possess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your arrival, was it your duty to analyse the strategic goals of the ABiH and HVO, both on arrival and during the time of your stay?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was part of our process to understand the situation in order to execute our mission. And as the second in command of the battalion, my major responsibilities, as well as being the deputy commander, were to coordinate the information and operational cells and to develop the situation reports for the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On information and intelligence coming to you, what view did you form about the approach of the ABiH in February 1993 and their approach towards alliance with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The unifying threat to Central Bosnia was posed by the Serb forces, and that threat was such that the only way the remaining area of Bosnia was going to be able to deny Serb aggression was for the Muslim and Croat forces to unite in an alliance which would give them sufficient fighting power to be able to defend Central Bosnia against the Serbs. If they were to try and do it individually, then the Serbs would able to destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the ABiH have any outside supporters or champions?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Within Europe, the ABiH had very few champions or supporters. Their support was largely based on their religion of Islam, and the Islamic world had great sympathy and support for the Bosnian Muslims. But that wasn't able to focus itself on immediate materiel support, although we were aware of considerable sums of money, both pledged and moved into Bosnia, to support the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO, what was their position so far as outside supporters was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The HVO were directly supported by Croatia, and within Europe, there was a large body of support within Germany for the Croat and Bosnian Croat cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did the Vance-Owen Plan affect the approach or objectives of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan affected not only the HVO, it also affected what was going on with the Serbs in other parts of Bosnia. But your specific question, the implementation or the likely implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan resulted in the creation of a series of cantons within Bosnia. And the one that most impacted on our area of responsibility, certainly in April '93, was that, I think, of canton 10, which was essentially centred on Vitez and Busovaca. And that likely implementation galvanised the HVO/Croat thinking as to how they were going to exist as a grouping post the Vance-Owen Plan, and there was a great deal of talk among military commanders and the general population as to the impact of this plan on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, about the Vance-Owen Plan, I should like to ask the witness, Colonel Watters, to tell us if the adoption of the plan and its acceptance by the HVO perhaps induced the HVO to think that they could take positions by force, which was accorded it by the Vance-Owen Plan, as the witness said. Was it planning to take these positions by force?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Before the 15th/16th of April, we thought this was a possibility, but we hadn't seen anything to indicate that this was imminent. Our main focus at that time was on what was happening in the Muslim pockets, where the Serbs, in -- I think it was western Bosnia, Srebrenica -- the Serbs themselves were trying to ethnically cleanse the Muslim population, because the Muslim population was driving the shape of the cantons in that part of Bosnia. I had a conversation in Serbia with a series of Serbian military commanders who explained to me that their offensive in Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje was designed to remove the Muslim majority population to enable the Serb minority, who owned 70 per cent of the land, to control the canton. It was that thinking and briefing from those Serb commanders that caused me to discuss and debate, after the events of the 15 and 16, that the Croat operations in Central Bosnia were mirroring what the Serbs were doing in other parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So specifically dealing with Judge Bennouna's question as to whether they felt they could take by force that which was accorded by the Vance-Owen Plan, in your judgement, did they think that at any stage, either before or after the 15th or 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I believed that they did think that they would be able to secure the boundaries and routes in and around canton 10 and routes to support canton 10 from Croatia proper, and I believe that is why they launched their offensive on the morning of the 16th of April. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to pause there, we're going to deal with that at the conclusion of your evidence, when the events leading up to it have been --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In -- the simple answer to the question, sir, is "yes." I and our team did not realise that prior to the 15th and 16th of April, but in analysing the situation during the offensive and after it, and in discussions with Croat and Muslim senior military commanders on the 21st of April, I was very clear in my mind that that is exactly what the Croats, the HVO, had attempted to do on the 15th/16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back to paragraph 6 of the summary at the end of the evidence. Before I turn to paragraph 7, on arrival, and as far as you could judge from your knowledge of what had happened before, was the fighting at maximum level, or was there something of a lull in activity?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, the period ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you arrived, was it at full force, the fighting, or was there something of a lull?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, when I arrived, there was a lull. There had been -- in November/December '92 there had been a major Serb offensive from Banja Luka down to Donji Vakuf and stopping at Turbe and Travnik, and that was the major focus of military activity around Christmas. Just after Christmas, and when I arrived, there was some fighting in the Kiseljak valley, between Busovaca and Kiseljak, which had ceased or was at a very low level, and our main preoccupation on my arrival was actually policing ceasefires in the Kiseljak valley. The main area within the Lasva Valley was generally peaceful, and our main focus, really, was the evacuation of refugees following the Serb offensive from Banja Luka and the fighting with the Serbs north of Travnik. So within Central Bosnia, essentially, it was moderately quiet, and other than occasional disagreements at the lower tactical level in the village, between the different ethnic groups in Central Bosnia, at the sort of tactical or strategic level, the alliance against the Serbs was generally in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following your arrival, did you meet Dario Kordic? If so, roughly how many times and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I met Mr. Kordic once in his headquarters in Busovaca, following the hijacking of a vehicle, and our liaison officer, Captain Foregrave, was endeavouring to solicit the support of Mr. Kordic to try and have the vehicle returned. I met him on another occasion, very briefly, in Busovaca, just on a general call when we went to see him. He was actually very busy in a meeting, and we didn't actually get to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the vehicle, tell us what happened in the end so far as that vehicle was concerned.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Right. There were several incidents, one before my arrival, with a soldier who had been abducted in Kiseljak, which Mr. Kordic arranged -- or at least, after speaking to him, the man was released; we believed Mr. Kordic had arranged that. And we would go to him or our liaison officers would go to him to resolve situations because of his obvious political influence in the area. There was a situation, I think it was in March '93, where a Dutch officer driving alone in his vehicle was apprehended at a Croat checkpoint, and he was beaten up, his weapon stolen and his vehicle stolen. Having failed to get the vehicle back, we sent a liaison officer to speak to Mr. Kordic, and Mr. Kordic said he would do what he could to have the vehicle returned, and shortly afterwards, the vehicle was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With or without the firearm?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Without any weapons, just the vehicle itself, with most things removed from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another incident involving an aid convoy?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There was a convoy that we had negotiated the movement of from Zenica to Travnik. The convoy was abducted at a Croat checkpoint at the Busovaca/Vitez road junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to interpose an objection here, a very short one. If we're dealing with paragraph 8, it appears that the witness is going to be invited to give hearsay several times removed about something that he was told that that person was told by a person at a checkpoint. And obviously that's double hearsay, or worse, and we object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear the background to the evidence and how it got to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Carry on, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The convoy was abducted. What essentially happened was the convoy commander, who is a young officer, his Warrior had anti-tank mines placed at the front and back of its tracks so he couldn't manoeuvre his Warrior, and then the Croat forces got onto the runningboards of the vehicles, smashed the window with their rifle butts, and put their rifles through the window and ordered the drivers to drive around the Warrior and up into Busovaca. I was in the operations room when this happened. I contacted the headquarters of Colonel Blaskic in Vitez, as we had negotiated with him, as the regional military commander of Croat forces, the safe passage of this convoy from Zenica to Travnik. He informed us that he would see what he could do, and we then waited. I then received a report over the radio, and I can't tell you who gave me the report, it was either the platoon commander or one of his other vehicles, that the soldiers at the checkpoint who were dressed in black uniforms, which was not the normal uniforms of the Croat forces, it was more the sort of special units, had said, when told that this convoy had the authority of Colonel Blaskic, that they didn't take their orders from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's precisely what we're talking about. We're talking about obviously comments which required interpretation. Those, in turn, were related to the unidentified source that Colonel Watters has just talked about, and that person is not available to be cross-examined, as far as we are aware, since he's not identified. How can we possibly challenge or evaluate the reliability of that testimony? So we object to it on the grounds of double-hearsay or worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if I've got this right. Colonel Watters, you were in the control room?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You received a report on the radio --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- from a platoon commander or somebody similar?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Through his company ops room, Sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Through the company ops room. The report was to the effect that the soldiers at the checkpoint were dressed in black uniforms and had said something about where they got their authority from?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, did you want to say something about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Well, there's more evidence that ties Kordic in with responsibility for this, including what he said himself later on, as we can see at the foot of paragraph 8. There's also the actions taken to release the convoy, which again fit with it. So the evidence is, in any event, under the Rules of this Tribunal, prima facie admissible, questions of weight, and the evidence overall will satisfy the Tribunal as to Kordic's responsibility. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear all the evidence on this point, and then we'll make a decision as to what, if any, should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The information that you received came from someone you can't now name?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I can't remember which of the platoon commanders in A Company or in Cheshire it was that was commanding the convoy that was abducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who led the convoy? Which officer had led that sad convoy?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: A platoon commander. I don't remember which one. We had nine of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you debrief him?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I spoke to him later to ascertain what he had done that had allowed the Croat checkpoint to abduct his convoy, because we had procedures designed to prevent that happening. In discussions with him, he had failed to enact those procedures, and I wrote an order reminding all company commanders to practice our procedures for securing convoys in the event of them being stopped at checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there anything said by him inconsistent with the intelligence you had that offered that the hijackers had said they wouldn't take orders from Blaskic but only from Kordic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The convoy commander had known that the authority for the convoy, which we had gone to quite a lot of trouble to plan because it was going from a Muslim town, through a Croat area, to a Muslim town and we expected there would be some difficulties with it, and he knew that the regional military commander, Colonel Blaskic, had given authority for this convoy to move through. And when the soldiers were confronted by the convoy commander with the fact that they had authority from Colonel Blaskic, the people at the checkpoint said to him they didn't take their orders from Colonel Blaskic, they took them from Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a consequence of what you learned, both over the radio and perhaps by debriefing the person commanding the convoy or leading the convoy, what next step did you take?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: We contacted Colonel Blaskic's headquarters, and they said there was really nothing they could do and suggested that we spoke to Mostar. I was commanding the battalion at that time, as the commanding officer was away. I ordered the officer commanding A Company to assemble a combat group and to be prepared to go to Busovaca and take back the convoy by force using a company of Warriors, and I set a deadline for him to launch his assault. I then spoke to our headquarters in Kiseljak and asked them to speak with General Petkovic in Mostar and try and get orders given from Mostar to Mr. Kordic in Busovaca to release the convoy before we attacked Busovaca to take the convoy back by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you know, did UN-HQ do what you asked of them?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I personally spoke with the headquarters. They had spoken with Colonel Petkovic's headquarters in Mostar, and they had assured United Nations headquarters that they would pass instructions immediately to Busovaca because it was in no one's interest for the United Nations to assault the Croat forces to capture a convoy that they had illegally taken. It was in no one's interest for this to happen, and they would ensure that the orders were given to Mr. Kordic to release the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the convoy released?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and Major Thomas, I think it was, or one of the liaison officers went to see Mr. Kordic, and he explained that the reason the convoy had been taken was to make a political point that there was an unfair distribution of aid between the Muslim communities and the Croat communities and he believed the Croat communities had been disadvantaged, and he had made his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was said to whom?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry, it wasn't at the time of huge significance, and I don't remember. It was either Major Thomas, now Colonel Thomas, or one of the liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It wasn't said to you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not by Mr. Kordic, no. I didn't go and see Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An error has crept into paragraph 8 and it shouldn't have been there, but it can be corrected. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the evidence on that point, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, Your Honour. First of all, the purported admission isn't an admission at all. Mr. Kordic, even according to this hearsay testimony that was given to Major Thomas, now Colonel Thomas, or someone else, says the reason the convoy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The reason the convoy had been taken was to make a political point. That's exactly what Colonel Watters said. He didn't say that he had ordered this convoy to be taken or that he had any culpability or responsibility for it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak slower, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One other point I would like to make is the perniciousness of receiving these offers of proof just minutes before trial. There's no statement in here, you'll notice, in any of the prior testimony. This witness has given hundreds of pages of testimony before this Tribunal. He's given a statement which is 23 pages long to the Prosecution. He actually prepared his own statement in 1994. There isn't a peep, not a word, about this in those statements or in his prior testimony. But the main point is, Your Honour, it's hearsay many times removed. This witness didn't hear it, he's not in a position to evaluate it, and I think that the alleged tie-in, the alleged admission, isn't an admission at all, by this witness's own testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many times removed is it, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many times removed is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: By my count, it looks like it's at least three times removed, Judge Robinson. It looks like the soldiers supposedly shouted something presumably in Croatian. Maybe it was translated. If it was translated, then that would be four times removed. But the soldiers shouted something to someone, who then reported it to the platoon commander or someone, who then reported it to Colonel Watters, so there's at least three levels of hearsay there and perhaps four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, unless the platoon commander heard it himself and reported it to Colonel Watters. No doubt these are matters which can be explored in cross-examination. We think this evidence is plainly admissible. Although it's hearsay, the Tribunal Rules permit hearsay to be given, and so that it's a question of weight very often. Here we note that this communication was given to this witness in the operations room and also in the very moments in which it was all happening. Now, whether these are matters which should be the subject of cross-examination is a matter for counsel, but they are plainly admissible. What weight we give to it, of course, will be a matter we'll have to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, what judgement did you form of Mr. Kordic's role in Central Bosnia from your encounters, brief though they were with him, and from intelligence coming to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I hate to be a pest, Your Honour, but I have to object to that. That's calling for an opinion from this witness based upon one meeting at which he spoke to Mr. Kordic, and I don't believe that this witness is competent to give any meaningful opinion about the subject of Mr. Kordic's alleged authority or leadership in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's look at it this way: Colonel, did you actually meet Mr. Kordic, first of all?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Sir, in his headquarters in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you said on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I went to his headquarters on two occasions. The second occasion, he was in a large meeting, and we got in, I saw him, but we didn't interrupt him because I don't know what was going on but it was obviously of great concern to him, so we left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the other occasion, you had a conversation with him, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was introduced to him by the then Captain Foregrave, having recently arrived as second in command of the battle group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, do you want to deal with that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may deal with the conversation, but there is also a lot of other evidence that will lead to the same general topic, and perhaps I can deal with it in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, that conversation, can you just help us with that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Really, it was just a general -- I can't recollect the exact detail of the conversation. It was an introduction. He was introduced to me as vice-president of HVO, a very influential man who had been to visit the battalion on several occasions, and Colonel Stewart had told me that he was politically influential within Central Bosnia and appeared to head up the political focus and Colonel Blaskic headed up the military focus, and they were the two Croat personalities of influence in our military area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next bits of evidence about chains of command, help us with this detail. At the time of your arrival, were you expecting necessarily trouble with the Croats, or the Muslims, or between them, or were you hoping for the possibility of conciliation and peaceful progress?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In my introductory briefings, I was briefed on the alliance. In my personal meetings with the various groups, there was no doubt that there were great tensions, there were very old wounds from previous fighting, there was a degree of distrust between the two communities, and that the lower the level one spoke, the less trust there was within the two military groupings and, in essence, there was very little love lost between the two communities, and their alliance appeared to be borne out of sort of mutual threat. But it certainly wasn't an alliance of friends. It was an alliance of antagonists, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that situation, what was your intention, so far as leading figures were concerned? Did you intend to get close to them, to get to know them, to keep them at arm's length? Explain.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: My specific role as the deputy commander was not to personally liaise with the commanders on a routine basis, other than when I was standing in as the commanding officer. That role was largely that of the commanding officer, and our modus operandi was for the liaison officers, six or so that we had appointed, to do that as their primary function, to get to know the military, political, and civic leaders within our area to facilitate negotiation by myself and the company commanders in the place of the commanding officer if he wasn't available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did those liaison officers report back to you and to the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Primarily, they would report back to the commanding officer and report back to me in his absence. I would obviously monitor the situation and sit in on those briefings with the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the situation which you found yourself, was it important or not to have an understanding of the chain or chains of command of other forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was very important to understand the structure of the indigenous forces in Central Bosnia so we knew where to interdict and at what level within the chain of command we needed to interdict to carry out our mission of facilitating the movement of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of information did you have to inform you of the chain of command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: We had a wide variety of sources, both human sources and other sources, to put together a structure of the military and political chains of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you form a view as to whether there was a unitary chain of command or not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There were two -- our understanding was that there were essentially two chains of command. There was a military chain of command and a political chain of command, which wasn't unusual; it's how it is in most European countries. Where it got a little confusing was the situation in Central Bosnia, where there would appear to be disagreement or contradiction between the political chain of command, focused on Mr. Kordic, and the military chain of command, focused on Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Confusion in what sense or -- sorry, disagreement or contradiction in what sense?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The fact that Colonel Blaskic would give instructions and assurances, as in the case of that convoy I referred to earlier, and those assurances wouldn't be manifested on the ground, and we would have to then go to Mostar to interdict the political chain of command and have direction given to Mr. Kordic. We couldn't go through Colonel Blaskic to Mr. Kordic, because he didn't appear to take his orders from him; which isn't unusual, because he wasn't a military person, although we would then see him wearing uniform and behaving like a soldier, and that caused us a degree of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll complete the contents of paragraph 9 when all the evidence is in. On the 13th of February, was there a meeting in Busovaca -- I beg your pardon, in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, in the French engineers' camp in Kakanj, yes, there was a meeting to address the ceasefire arrangements following the fighting in January in the Kiseljak valley, between Busovaca and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The result of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The result of that meeting was a series of ceasefire agreements and agreements on our part to position soldiers in their Warriors at certain key bridges and junctions on the road to verify the ceasefire and to facilitate the free passage of Muslims and Croats between -- essentially along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, the next event I want you to deal with, had you been to Vitez, and did you return from Vitez to learn of a visit paid to Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. There had been a visit to Travnik by Mr. Boban, and the general Muslim population were very nervous and alarmed, as Mr. Boban had incited, in their words, the Croat population to be manifestly more Croat and less of an alliance. One particular point he had highlighted was the lack of Croat flags in Travnik, and he had told the Croat leaders of Travnik that they were to fly more Croat flags and manifest their identity to a greater extent. This resulted in a few nights of civil disturbance, during which several Muslim youths were shot -- I can't remember the exact number -- attempting to either take down flags or banners that had been put up in Travnik. It generally sort of unsettled the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then come to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, could you tell us, since you spoke about the chain of command, the chain of command, where is -- we heard about Colonel Blaskic, about Mr. Kordic; where would you say -- what was Mr. Boban's place in that chain of command? Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Boban was a senior political figure within the Croat government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... take on military uniform or have any apparent military rank?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he ever, to your knowledge, have direct military control of people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Are you talking about Boban?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Boban, yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not in my judgement, and Mr. Boban operated at a level sort of higher than BritBat was, in all honesty, interested in, until he came into our area of responsibility in Central Bosnia. So he wasn't a figure that I or BritBat had any requirement to track or be specifically interested in, other than being aware that he was a senior and very influential figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to the 15th and 16th of April. There had been the ceasefire. If you can identify or encapsulate the state of expectation on the 15th, perhaps you would do so; and if you can't, we'll just move to the facts.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The -- I need to put it, really, in context. Our major focus was with our company group in Tuzla, where we were involved in the evacuation of refugees from Srebrenica. On the 15th, there was a kidnapping in Zenica of the HVO commander -- I think Commander Totic was his name -- and there had been the murder of his bodyguards in a vehicle. Colonel Stewart went from Vitez to Zenica to investigate the situation and ensure that this didn't lead to a complete breakdown between the Muslim and Croat peoples in Zenica. But we considered this to be a very serious incident. We didn't understand it, and we were endeavouring to speak to the 3rd Corps commander -- which is why Colonel Stewart went to Zenica -- Hadzihasanovic, to establish what on earth was going on, basically. And so that was the situation. So it was tense, as an immediate result of this -- this act, terrorist act in Zenica, and the kidnapping of the HVO commander. And that was essentially the situation, with most of our effort, as I say, focused in the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in north, on which troops?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, our own company group in Tuzla, and the reinforcement, specifically helicopters, that we were using, with our own people in them, to go into Srebrenica to evacuate the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we come to the 16th. Commander Colonel Stewart had gone to Zenica; did he stay in Zenica that night?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. We spoke on the phone on the evening of the 15th and decided that it was too dangerous for him to risk coming back in the dark, as the situation was very tense following the kidnapping of Mr. Totic, and he should remain in Zenica overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had there been an ultimatum delivered in relation to Totic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, which was what had created the tenseness, and that was if Mr. Totic wasn't recovered very quickly, then the HVO would evacuate the Croat people from Zenica, which was a major situation. And so, suddenly, if you like, our focus very quickly turned from Tuzla back down into Central Bosnia, as this situation appeared to be very quickly gaining momentum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evacuation of the Croat population of Zenica suggesting what sort of consequence?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, a major schism and breakdown in the alliance between the Croats and the Muslims, and the possibility of returning to full-scale fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th of April, an event that, as I think you know, isn't in the summary, but just tell us about it: 2.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, very early in the morning; 2.00, 1.30, something like that, I had only just gone to bed, and I was woken up to be told that there were some journalists in our base in Vitez who had just been forced from their accommodation and were in state of considerable shock, and so I came down to speak to them. They said that they had been staying in the -- a sort of guest house just between our school and Vitez. There was a bear in a cage at this boarding house, sort of a small hotel, which is how we knew it, the hotel with the bear in the garden. They had been staying there, and in the very early hours of the morning, the owners -- who were Muslim -- of the boarding house had been arrested by Croat soldiers wearing balaclavas, their faces covered, and the journalists were told that if they didn't leave, they would be killed, and they weren't to take their possessions, they were just to go. So they got into their car and drove to our base. It was just a very strange incident, and on top of what was going on in Zenica, was of considerable concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you in due course receive reports of shelling?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah. Shortly afterwards, we got reports -- initially, I think, from the Dutch transport squadron based near Vitez -- that there was shelling in the town of Vitez. We then had reports from our own Echelon logistic base outside Vitez that there was shelling. And this was unusual. It was quite common in the night for there to be small arms firing, but very unusual for there to be mortar or shell fire, and certainly, of the sustained frequency that was being reported to us, meant that something unusual and very large was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was BritBat able to assess from where the shells came? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Immediately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subsequently?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: By looking where they were falling, which was in the Muslim areas of Kruscica and Vitez, it made obvious sense that they were being fired by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, at that time, who had authority to deal with this scale of attack on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry, there was one other -- there was a large artillery piece in a quarry that I think we called -- or that was called "Bertha," or something, which was a Croat artillery piece that was also firing, and we, as a -- our reconnaissance units identified that. So that was a single piece that we knew was firing. The use of artillery was controlled at the regional level of command, which would be Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What steps did you take on discovering this shelling was taking place?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I ordered reconnaissance parties to go out to Vitez and the environs to try and establish what was happening and to try and -- and sent the liaison officers to make contact with the Muslim commander in Vitez and the Croat commander in Vitez to ask them what on earth was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you achieve any contact with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: We couldn't speak to Colonel Blaskic, who wasn't available. We spoke to the Vitez Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That was -- Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see him yourself, or did somebody else see him?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I saw him later that morning, at 9.00, half past 9.00, in his headquarters in the cinema in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I mean, I did; let me think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think there's any challenge to that. What about the Muslims: Did you make any contact with Muslim commanders?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I went also to see the Muslim commander in Vitez, having spoken with the Croat commander -- I think it was that way around -- and invited them to attend a ceasefire meeting in Vitez school at 12.00 on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At your first contact with the Vitez Brigade commander, can you help us with what, if anything, he said or what his response was to your concerns?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: His response was to agree to come to a ceasefire meeting. Both sides said the others were attacking them. From my own observations within the town and the environs, it was no doubt that the HVO forces had the upper hand, and most of the destruction and casualties and dead people I saw were in the Muslim areas of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you look first, I think, at some photographs -- I hope various exhibits have been distributed to everyone. They're slightly out of order; in fact, they're significantly out of order, because they have been given an order that matches their numbering, but that's not in fact the appropriate order. If we go, please, to the second-to-last photograph from the album, 2007. It may be that -- yes. Is this an appropriate photograph of this part of your testimony, Colonel, or not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I took that photograph myself, from the turret of my Warrior, as I was driving into Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it shows, simply ... ?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It shows the town and columns of smoke coming up from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we come back, in this little collection of paragraphs, one photograph, again, is Z1749 appropriate to this stage of your testimony, to make sure I've got it right? Colonel, is this an appropriate photograph for this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's representative of what I saw. I couldn't take any photographs within most of Vitez itself because we were being fired at, and so I had closed down my Warrior. On the far side of Vitez, going off down towards Dubravica, just past the Catholic cemetery, as I turned out of the bottom of the hill, there were a line of bodies, at the entrance to some houses, that had been lined up along the side of the road, and I took a quick photograph of them as I went past. That looks like it's the photograph, or very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These bodies appear to be in a line. Anything significant in that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Up till then, the bodies we had seen were lying in the street, hanging out of windows in buildings. These bodies struck me as quite shocking. It's a strange emotion, but because they had been sort of neatly lined up at the bottom of a drive, in a line, they appeared to be almost a statement. And it wasn't unusual for us to see sort of bodies displayed as warnings or as political statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just deal with that, as a small topic, here. It's not covered in the summary, but it's a topic I was going to get you to deal with. The display of dead bodies, over the period of time that you were there, to what degree did you see this or some kinds of display?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: On several occasions. Bodies that had been mutilated or having been sort of -- the people killed, the bodies themselves mutilated, and either left as a demonstration of the work of the perpetrators, and these bodies themselves acted as a huge and understandable provocation for the continuing of a sort of cycle of revenge and killing. Sometimes they were just left on the field of battle or in the village that had been attacked, and on other occasions they were more starkly on display. There was a specific body, that we could actually see from our camp, which appeared, which had been quite hideously disfigured and tied to a lamppost just on the hill overlooking our camp. We were often beseeched by both sides to retrieve these bodies from fields of battle, because to do it themselves was obviously very dangerous; and so on several occasions the commanding officer agreed to retrieve bodies to reduce the tension in a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help us with this from your experience, as it may help, and it may be interesting, but in what other countries and theatres have you been, if any, where you've seen this sort of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In varying degrees, but the only country that I've served in as a soldier where I've seen the use of sort of ritualistic murder to make statements was probably in Africa during the Rhodesian war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at Z2240, please, which is the aerial photograph of Vitez. You may not have had enough time to review this photograph since you arrived, this aerial photograph, since you arrived yesterday, but I think you can probably help us with it. This has been marked on a previous occasion, and it may be marked by you. If so, can you say as much and tell us what the markings show?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I certainly did mark an air photograph of Vitez to show my route in on the morning of the 16th, which is here (indicating). And also later, I think it was on the evening of the 16th, at the request of the Muslim forces and supported by Colonel Blaskic, I took a group up into Kruscica to retrieve some wounded people from the fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The view from the turret taken roughly where?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was roughly about -- about here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's towards the bottom -- well, the main road --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The main road into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Travelling up on this plan?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The bodies, either similar to or exactly as photographed in Z1749, can you tell us where they were lain out?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: About here, just below the cemetery. I think the cemetery was about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that is the top left-hand part?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah. It's quite -- quite difficult to see. There were considerable numbers of bodies in Stari Vitez, in the southern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these the ones hanging from windows and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: And in buildings and by the side of the road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So you made contact with the commanders, you did your tour of Vitez, and what did you notice of the areas inhabited by Croats, typically?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was stark, in that the majority of the fighting went up to the Hotel Vitez, which was actually the HVO headquarters of Colonel Blaskic. And there was a sort of buffer zone, about 100 or 200 metres, between the Hotel Vitez, up here (indicating), and Stari Vitez, and there was a definite front line of defence which the Muslims were holding, and the majority of the physical destruction of buildings was in the Muslim quarter. And as you passed the Hotel Vitez and went into the northern suburbs, which were the Croat side of the town, although the place was utterly deserted and there wasn't anything on the streets -- other than some mines; parts of the road had been mined -- it was as if nothing was going on. It was -- the buildings hadn't been touched, and it was as if you could draw a line through the town, and on one side there was fighting and on the other side there wasn't fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, that same day, receive reports of fighting elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive reports of fighting up and down the Lasva Valley, focused on most of the small Muslim villages and hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you name the ones of which you heard reports?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, at Ahmici -- I'm sorry, I mean the names don't stay in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But up and down the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mostly on the small Muslim villages and hamlets. What about the --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: We did send patrols to these various places, and our Warriors evacuated civilians from these areas of fighting for most of the 16th and 17th and moved them to wherever the ethnic grouping was that they belonged to, whether it be into Vitez or into Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What state of preparedness was the ABiH seen by you to have been in?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: My professional judgement was that they had been taken by surprise at the scale, coordination, and sort of momentum of the HVO attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up on the word "coordination", what, if anything, did that indicate to you as to the fighting that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, it was the first time that I had witnessed a coordinated offensive in the area. We had seen lots of sort of punch-ups between small communities, different villages, but we hadn't seen a coordinated offensive where there were attacks happening simultaneously up and down the valley and being reported to us at the same time. If you can imagine, the morning of the 16th was a very, very confusing situation, as we were getting dozens of reports from the United Nations, the UNHCR, the HVO, and the BiH and our own reconnaissance forces, of fighting up and down the valley north of Kiseljak, Jelinak, Kruscica, Novi Travnik, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What targets, military or otherwise, were the object of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: As the 16th and the 17th passed, the objective of all the fighting appeared to be at the Muslim villages. These were villages in which the Muslim people live and the men of those villages were soldiers, and the tradition was that soldiers having come from the front line took their weapons home with them, and so within the villages, that the men would be armed. But I wouldn't describe them as military objectives. They were villages in which men, women, and children lived, and the men were fighters and at that point, we thought, allies of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of these attacks, where was the concentration of forces that were engaged in fighting elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The majority of the 3rd Corps, which was the Muslim main military formation for that part of Bosnia, was, like our own attention, largely focused on the Serbs and the fighting in the pockets and reinforcing, I think it was, 5th Corps in Travnik, and so there were no Muslim reserves in Zenica and in the environs. The 3rd Corps, which was based on Zenica, was involved in fighting with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting you had arranged, who attended?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Is this the meeting on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, no, on the 15th or 16th.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: On the morning of?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the 16th, yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: At lunchtime. It was attended by the Muslim commander and representatives of the Croat commander. I don't think, in the end, he came. I could be wrong. I don't think he came. I think he sent a couple of representatives, although he may have appeared for a short time, because I do have a recollection of talking and finding it how strange that two people who were fighting each other could sit down in my office and have a very sane conversation. So I think he may have appeared, and at a later part of the meeting or at a subsequent meeting, he didn't appear and sent representatives. I'm afraid I'm a little confused in my memory there, but I certainly have a recollection of speaking to both of them and agreeing that what was happening was in nobody's interest, and again not quite realising the scale of what was happening, believing it was confined largely on the morning of the 16th to Vitez and was just a major fallout in Vitez and a little bit of Kruscica, that we would be able, as three sort of sane human beings, to actually bring this madness to an end. That was my thinking at lunchtime on the 16th. It transpired to be very naive thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the representative of the Muslims prepared, willing, or anxious to sign a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he was very anxious and was very agitated. He was -- I don't know how long he thought he could hold out, but I certainly got the feeling that he believed his ability to hold out was finite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the attitude of either the commander from Vitez or his representatives to a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Less tense but still very concerned at what was happening within the town of Vitez. I mean he didn't appear to be taking any satisfaction from what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was a ceasefire formally arranged?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it implemented?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently go to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose headquarters were there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was a Muslim headquarters, and the reason I went to Kruscica was the Muslims, I think as a precondition to their ceasefire, required the evacuation of some women and children casualties, because the Croat forces had cut the road to Kruscica here (indicating) and also the side road to Kruscica here (indicating), and so the Muslim forces were unable to evacuate their casualties to the medical aid in Novi Travnik, or in Stari Vitez, or in Travnik, and so they were isolated within Kruscica and couldn't evacuate their casualties. So we were asked, and it was agreed by the HVO as a humanitarian act, that we would be able to go into Kruscica and retrieve these casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you see of fighting that was going on or had been going on at that village?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There was considerable fighting. There was very little fighting within Vitez itself in the evening when I went up, and we entered Kruscica just after last light and there was a great deal of RPG 7 mortar and small-arms fire coming from the high ground and woods here (indicating) into the village. And there was artillery and mortars, I couldn't tell which, just large explosions in the village, which was destroying houses. I went to the Muslim headquarters -- our vehicles were hit several times coming in, but only by small-arms fire -- and they gave me a guide to take me to the house where the casualties were. It transpired, in fact, all the casualties were men, they weren't women. They were in civilian clothes, and we evacuated them anyway, put them in our vehicles. I had taken half a dozen Warriors and half a dozen armoured ambulances, and we evacuated these people and then made our way back down -- I think I actually took that route (indicating) back down into Vitez through the minefield here and then along the sort of ring road around Vitez back to our own base, and then took the casualties on, in our ambulances, to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any military reason for the shelling that was taking place? Could you identify any military target in that part of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was like the other areas, there was a Muslim headquarters there, which I visited, which was a military headquarters with radios and, you know, the normal paraphernalia of a headquarters, and the actual assault was on the village itself. But there was also fire being returned from some of the houses, and so there was no doubt that the Muslim forces within Kruscica were defending the village. But there was a far-greater fire coming into the village than was leaving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What effect, if any, did this attack have on the population?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, apart from sort of killing and injuring them, I mean the population themselves were quite traumatised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know if they stayed there or if they moved?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. They were sheltering in their cellars when I went there. Whether they subsequently moved out of the village or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's 11.00. If you're moving to another topic, that might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour. Colonel, will you please remember, in this and any other adjournments, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that does include the Prosecution, not to speak to anybody until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, Colonel, were you informed by Blaskic about a peace document that had been signed?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. There had been a peace document signed at the very highest level, allegedly, and this peace document Colonel Blaskic said required a ceasefire to be imposed. We had not heard about this document initially through our own chain of command, and we made enquires about it and established that such a document did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The attitude of the HVO to this document and its contents, apparently?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The HVO's attitude was the document was binding to themselves and the BiH and required an immediate cessation of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did it involve, so far as canton 10 was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, in essence, if the ceasefire had been implemented on the 18th, it would have consolidated the gains made by the HVO forces after their offensive on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The attitude of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The Muslims initially denied knowledge of the document and certainly ignored the document and didn't refer to it or give it any credibility until a meeting. On the day of the 20th, we heard they were sending a delegation on the 21st to a peace conference in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, on the 18th and 19th, the ABiH, who had, in your judgement, been unprepared for what happened, were doing what?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They were launching -- having the centres of Muslim population largely held out or, having said that, contracted slightly, and the HVO had gained control of key routes and key junctions, and the actual core areas of the Muslim population had been able to defend themselves, with some exceptions of ethnic cleansing and, as we later discovered, wholesale destruction of villages along the Lasva Valley. But there was still the key areas of Kruscica, Stari Vitez, and villages down the Kiseljak valley were still actually holding out. The 3rd Corps launched a counteroffensive out of Vitez -- out of Zenica, linked up with these isolated Muslim enclaves, and by the 20th had actually rolled back most of the HVO gains and were in a very strong position on the evening of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 18th, was there a report of a truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard about that, so we can deal with it quite shortly.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there many killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, there were, and also it caused quite a wholesale evacuation of civilians from Stari Vitez, who came up to our echelon base just outside Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your judgement of this as what sort of an act?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was a straightforward act of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any legitimate military objective in it at all?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Only probably to destroy the will of the people of Stari Vitez to resist and to remain there and by destroying their religion sites and, in so doing, possibly hoping to destroy their will. But one couldn't call the murdering of men, women, and children as a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 21. On the 19th of April, the shelling of Zenica. Your judgement about that. First of all, the calibre of artillery and its place of origin?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was large-calibre artillery. We estimated probably about 155 millimetres, from the examination of the strike sites in Zenica and also the range at which we believed this artillery had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any Serb artillery within that range?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No. The nearest Serb artillery we knew about -- and I can't say there wasn't some Serb artillery, but if there was Serb artillery within range, it would have had to move through the Croat-Muslim lines to have got in range, so behind the Serb lines, on our analysis, we couldn't identify any gun positions that could be in range of Zenica, given our knowledge of the Serbian artillery characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what, if anything, was this an apparent reaction, this shelling?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The shelling coincided with the 3rd Corps counteroffensive which had taken control or re-established control of some of their former positions and had, in essence, isolated or was in danger of isolating the towns of Busovaca and Vitez. It was my judgement and our judgement that the firing on Zenica, which I think killed 13 people, of artillery was a demonstration by the HVO that although with the combat power available to them in the Lasva Valley, they were unable to hold back the Muslim counterattack, they had the strategic means to cause considerable damage to the Muslim people. The shelling of Zenica was a demonstration of their ability to continue to inflict considerable damage on the Muslim people, even though at the time they were unable to defend the attack -- unable to prevent the Muslim forces from capturing the key junctioning and routes around Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any legitimate military target that you could identify? If not, to what did you liken this attack?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Zenica was certainly not a military target. I mean it was a densely-populated civilian large town, small city, even more densely populated following the fighting on the 16th to 19th of April, as most of the refugees from the Muslim areas in the Lasva Valley had actually moved into Zenica. I mean I think it's simply likened to a demonstration of the seriousness and intent the HVO had to go down fighting if they were forced to defend Vitez and Busovaca. If one was to draw an analogy, it was a -- no, I think I'll leave it there. It is simply the fact that they showed that although they were unable to defend in the field at that time, they possessed the capability to cause horrendous casualties and damage and make the capturing of Busovaca and Vitez not worth the loss to the Muslim and BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At about this time, was Blaskic saying things about the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: At this time, and more intensely later on, we were being bombarded from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters with a series of faxes and telephone calls accusing us of a wide range of crimes, from desecrating the Catholic church in Vitez, which is patently ridiculous, and equally ridiculous to the transporting of Muslim soldiers and transporting weapons to the Muslims fighting in their isolated areas. Those were an orchestrated propaganda campaign by the HVO against BritBat to discredit us and discredit the efforts we were taking to bring the situation under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a short clip of a video of Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's part of Z162,2, if that could be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One brief point, Your Honour: May we know the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: April the what, though?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think I can be precise. If I can, I will be. (Videotape played) I only want to talk about things which we can prove. One thing we are certain of is that twice, some people from UNPROFOR, I don't want to accuse all of UNPROFOR or the British, but unfortunately some did transport arms to the Muslims in their APCs to the villages where we were attacked. We gave proof of it to our commander, which he took to Mostar. He can show you, if you want to take pictures to prove that the arms were made in Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did the things being said by Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please. Microphone for Mr. Nice. Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did the things you were told by Blaskic, or had received in faxes, compare to what you have just heard?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Along very similar lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Although, on occasion, far more specific than Mr. Kordic was in that video about it actually being specifically BritBat that were doing it as opposed to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. What was, to your knowledge, the HVO's communications systems potential?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The HVO appeared to have quite reasonable communications, certainly within their command structure. The commanders that I met would either carry radio -- walkie-talkie-type radios or mobile phones, and they would appear to be in constant contact with their headquarters. During the period of the HVO offensive, all our phones went down, and the only time our phones came live was when we were phoned up or faxed by the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When they needed to contact you by those electronic means, did they appear to have any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No. They were obviously controlling the telephone systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, did you make a visit with the UNHCR official?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Zenica and escorted back a UNHCR official, in a small convoy of vehicles, from Zenica back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think -- may the witness have Z1946, please, which is a full aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The aerial photographs don't ordinarily face north/south, Colonel. You're probably adept at reading maps from all points of the compass, but if I put this one down north/south, it may generally help our attention, if you can orientate it north/south. Can you? Don't worry if you can't. Well, we lose the advantage with the labels, but that doesn't matter; we can read them sideways.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to have it that way up. It makes no difference to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In which case, tell us a little more about this.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: This is the road down the Lasva Valley, from Zenica down to Vitez.
