The Bungalow, which is a term that was a colloquial term for a military police or HOS-type unit that was stationed here, just outside Vitez, and who were characteristically dressed differently from the remainder of the HVO, in that they tended to wear black uniforms and generally looked sort of more efficient and capable, and we had observed them training and zeroing their rifles, et cetera, in the environs of the Bungalow for many weeks. We came across them ethnically cleansing a group of houses up here. What exactly happened was we were coming down the road, and as our Warriors, and my Warrior leading, came around the corner, a group of women and children ran into the road and sat down on the road so we couldn't pass. We dismounted from our Warriors and through an interpreter inquired what was going on. The women were quite frantic, and explained that the HVO were taking their houses and were going to kill the men. I went to speak to the commander of the unit that was conducting this operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there, do you know the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember. It was the unit that was based in the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: And asked him what the hell he thought he was doing. He said that they needed these buildings for Croat refugees, these houses, and that his orders were to clear the Muslim population. I asked him then why he had taken the -- sort of teenage boys and old men as prisoners, and he said they were his orders, and that they were to be taken away, but the women and children could leave with us in our vehicles. Obviously the women and children didn't want to leave without their men, and told us that the men were to be killed, and told us that if they -- they were told if they didn't leave the buildings themselves, the HVO soldiers had told them they were going to kill them. So it was obviously a very fractious situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Resolved how?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I spoke to the HVO commander and told him that he wasn't going to take the men prisoners, and we were going to evacuate the women and children and the men and take them to a place of safety, and that I would report this to the United Nations and also to Colonel Blaskic. In the end, we came to a compromise. I made it very clear to him that I was not leaving until we had resolved the situation, and we came to a compromise whereby the women and children could leave with us in our vehicles, whereas the men would have to leave on foot. And we remained in the area with these soldiers while the men made their way on foot to Zenica, and then we took the women and children to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The BritBat Echelon garage, whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That was on the road leading out of Vitez towards Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, was there a gathering of refugees there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was just after the truck bomb had exploded, and there were a group of refugees that had gathered seeking sanctuary. We didn't have the authority or the mandate to bring refugees into our bases, as it would compromise our role as part of the United Nations, but we did arrange with the UNHCR for these people to be evacuated to Zenica. While they were sheltering against the side of our base, they were opened fire at by snipers from adjacent houses. Several of them were hit and a couple killed. We positioned some armoured vehicles between the houses and the refugees and mounted an assault on the houses that had contained the snipers and captured the snipers. These we arrested and then informed Colonel Blaskic what was happening and asked him to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just Blaskic, or anybody else that you informed?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: We might have -- well, we certainly informed our own chain of command. We probably spoke to the brigade commander in -- the town commander in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the reaction of Blaskic, and/or the town commander in Vitez, to your intention to fire at snipers, or the fact that you had already done so?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In all honesty, I was a little concerned, because after this bombardment of propaganda, that we were actually taking the side of the Muslims against the Croats, the fact that we had now actually attacked some Croat soldiers in some ways really fed this ridiculous propaganda war, which is why I was keen to speak to the HVO and explain to them why we had done it. Colonel Blaskic was actually supportive of what we had done, and said that those soldiers weren't following his orders, and that if it happened again we should do it again; we should continue to protect these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reaction of the town commander, if you can help us?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I can't remember the detail of it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 21st of April, did you see some prisoners with their hands tied?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. I was coming from Zenica down the Dubravica road, or the mountain road, as we used to call it, and there were a group of Muslim men, with their hands tied behind their back, being escorted to what we later discovered was a prison camp in Dubravica. And we were told by the ICRC that they had been used to dig trenches for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see the trenches?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They were on the -- above the town of Dubravica, facing up the hill towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And whose trenches were they, by what process of calculation or deduction?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They were HVO, because the soldiers carrying rifles in the trenches, around the trenches, and guarding these prisoners, were all HVO, wearing HVO badges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 21st of April, was there a ceasefire meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, on the 21st of April, there was a ceasefire meeting arranged by the U.N. headquarters in Kiseljak, and the participants were the HVO and the BiH. The meeting was chaired by Ambassador Thebault from the ECMM commission, and in the absence of the commanding officer, I was the military representative at the ceasefire meeting. The HVO were represented by General Petkovic and Colonel Blaskic, and the BiH were represented by General Halilovic and Mr. Merdan, who was the 3rd BiH Corps' deputy commander, because the corps commander himself was unavailable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to the second sentence of paragraph 26 in a minute. But in the course of this meeting, did you or did someone seek reassurances or assurances from Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The structure of the meeting was that Ambassador Thebault essentially established a willingness on both sides for a ceasefire and a genuine desire for peace and a genuine desire to enforce a ceasefire. Having done that, he then handed the meeting over to me to establish the details of the ceasefire, and I suggested that we adjourn to two different rooms. And we put some maps on the table, and the BiH marked on the maps their positions and the HVO marked on the maps their positions, and from that we would work out a methodology of imposing a workable ceasefire. Having done that and established what was a potentially workable plan, my main concern was the ability of Colonel Blaskic to deliver this plan, given the fact that in the past, his orders and assurances to us had been overturned by Mr. Kordic. And so I asked General Petkovic if the plan that he had agreed and signed up to, to be implemented by Colonel Blaskic, would be overturned or interfered with by Mr. Kordic, and General Petkovic said that Mr. Kordic would obey his orders and not interfere with the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Kordic making any contact with those taking part in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not directly, to my knowledge. There were reports that Mr. Kordic had become increasingly alarmed, understandably so, as Busovaca was essentially cut off and then surrounded by Muslim forces. And later, when we learned of the massacre in Ahmici and some of the other villages around, I understood Mr. Kordic's concern, if he knew about those. There would be very little doubt in his mind as to what the Muslims would do if they decided to take Busovaca. There was no monopoly on either side for sort of outrageous acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second sentence. Did you have an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Different interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I had an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a time when Petkovic and Blaskic were speaking together?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There was an aside. The full consequences, at the time I didn't really take on board, were General Petkovic was giving Colonel Blaskic a severe talking to and was obviously very annoyed over something, and the gist of the conversation, translated to me by the interpreter, was essentially were things under control, and Blaskic said, yes, they were under control. And Petkovic said something along the lines, "Well, they better be." I found it odd, when translated to me, A; the impact it had made on the interpreter, who was shaking because he had heard this exchange, and, secondly; that it was a bit ridiculous for Blaskic to say things were in control when his forces were being mopped up and rolled up by the Muslims. With hindsight later, when Ahmici unfolded, I interpreted that conversation in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you, for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I presumed and interpreted the conversation, and understood then the absolute terror on the part of my interpreter that he had been privy to this conversation, that what actually they were talking about were the massacres that had been conducted and whether they, themselves, were under control or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a map on the easel. It will have to be given a new number, because although it's similar to a map that the witness marked in an earlier trial, it's a fresh marking. And therefore Z2618, which you may have in your bundles of which comes from the earlier trial, is to be distinguished from this, which should become 2618,1. I wonder if the witness could stand and very kindly take a pointer, and if the map is sufficiently visible, either at a distance or by use -- or on the screen, at this stage simply point out where the various lines of withdrawal and so on were agreed at this meeting. Now, I don't know whether the -- I haven't tried this before. Does the equipment allow us to focus on the map so that it comes up on the screen? I wonder if that can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could the technical staff photograph the large map, please, not Mr. Nice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at this map in a little more detail in a few minutes, but just for the time being, if the camera could go up just a little bit, please, to the top. Thank you so much. Could you please just point out the towns? They don't show up very visibly at the moment on the map. Just remind us, what's what at the top part?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. Zenica (indicating), a largely Muslim town; Vitez (indicating), a largely Croat town; Busovaca (indicating), a largely Croat town; Kacuni (indicating) and down to Kiseljak (indicating). So when I've referred to the Kiseljak Valley, I've meant here (indicating). The Lasva Valley follows the River Lasva here (indicating), with the main areas of interest to us being the mountain road down into Dubravica here (indicating) -- sorry, that's there (indicating) -- the junction here where the Kiseljak road out of Busovaca meets the Lasva Valley road (indicating), Vitez (indicating), then the main junction on the way to Travnik (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. Those are your points of interest, and we will come back to looking at some of those. For the time being, we see there are three blue marks, blue lines, on the map. Can you explain those, please?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. What they represent was the agreed lines of separation that I negotiated with the HVO and the BiH. This line here (indicating) --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The southern line?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The southern line, south of the Lasva Valley road, was the line behind which the Croat forces were to withdraw within 24 hours of the ceasefire being agreed, and the line marked "Alpha" here (indicating), the northern line, is the line behind which the BiH forces were to withdraw within 24 hours, and the second line was the line with which the BiH were to withdraw within 48 hours back into Zenica (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The northernmost line?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The northernmost line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you remind the Chamber where, in relation to those lines, Ahmici itself is?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Ahmici is there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it lies between the southernmost and the centre line?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, in what we call the zone of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would like to take your seat again for a moment. It was within that zone of separation that Ahmici fell. Just tell us, what was the process whereby the massacre at Ahmici was discovered?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The commanding officer led the initial reconnaissance force to establish, 24 hours after the agreed ceasefire, that the Croats had moved south of the southern line and the Muslim forces had moved north of line Alpha. When moving on the high ground south of line Alpha, Colonel Stewart found groups of Muslim soldiers who patently were south of line Alpha. When he asked them why they hadn't followed the orders of command of 3rd Corps and General Halilovic and moved north of line Alpha, they said to him that they weren't moving because of the massacre in Ahmici. Although we had heard and knew of fighting in Ahmici, and indeed one of our Warriors had evacuated civilian women and children from Ahmici, we weren't aware that there had been a massacre or any greater degree of fighting in Ahmici than there had been in the other towns along the valley, and so Colonel Stewart said that, initially frankly disbelieving and thinking that the BiH were prevaricating, Colonel Stewart said, "Well, I will go and personally check the village of Ahmici and then come back and report to you." So he moved down into the village and found that indeed there had been a massacre there and there were bodies, and the vast majority, if not all of the Muslim houses in the village, had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, I think, visited Ahmici on at least two days, the 22nd and 24th of April, for the recovery of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Initially, I went on a reconnaissance. Following Colonel Stewart's return, he was in a considerable state of sort of anger and shock, and I led another reconnaissance party back to the village to confirm what he had seen and also to further explore the extent of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were photographs taken, I think, by either you and others?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be so good, we can go quite swiftly through the small album, and on this occasion we can start at the beginning. For public record purposes, they must just be briefly laid on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Rather than me interrupt, you can probably, as it were, deal with them yourself, Colonel, giving the Chamber time enough to understand the points you're making, starting with Z1504.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There was one particular house that at that point had the majority of the bodies that we had, to date, discovered, and this is the entrance to that house (indicating), where there was a body that we thought to be a man lying in the entrance to the house. The house itself had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: This is a picture in the cellar of the same house that the first picture was at the entrance to. This is in the cellar, where there were a number of bodies among debris in the cellar, and this is one of those bodies (indicating). You can see the shape of the head (indicating) and the torso, and these bodies had also been burnt.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's another angle of the same photograph that's just preceded it.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: These are more bodies, and this is one of the walls of the cellar here (indicating), and there were a line of bullet strike marks against the wall and what we took to be blood on the wall of the building -- of the cellar, and there were a line of bodies in front of this wall which had also been burnt.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That, I think, is another shot in the cellar. It's quite difficult to tell. I mean that's certainly a skull (indicating), and I think it certainly looks like it's a shot from the cellar.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's another shot in the cellar. If you look very carefully, you can see a rib cage here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's a similar picture to the two before, where you can see the skull against an upturned sink or something here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1511, it would be same again, I think.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's another body in the cellar that was close to the wall where there's sort of the blood on the wall here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's another picture of bodies in the cellar. You can see the rib cages.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: This is another house. The pattern of destruction in most of the houses was very similar, in that the houses had been burned and either blown up and the roofs dropped into the bottom storey of the house or, in a few instances, the house were left like the house we've just seen, and within the debris of some of the houses, there were charred human remains, which we took to be human remains, which later proved to be human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here I think you can see a particular human remain, if you look?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see part of a rib cage there (indicating), part of a torso.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The photograph again at 1515?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the same house.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That -- if I remember it, we walked around several of the houses, and one had a rib cage in it and the other one had a skull. That might be the one with the skull, but I can't see it clearly from that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1517, the felled mosque minaret?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's the part of Ahmici that abuts the main Lasva Valley road, where the minaret had been blown up and dropped on top of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Run through to 1520.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's a close-up. You can see the reinforced concrete and steel that had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1521, basically --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. More of the same, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just go on to 1521. There's the removal of a body, presumably?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. That was removing bodies from that cellar and the house, which we conducted several days later as parts of a military operation. We were asked to do this by the BiH authorities, as they didn't feel it was safe for them to go and retrieve the bodies themselves.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's a picture looking into the house that the bodies were in the cellar, and you can see the body on the stairs (indicating) there was a close-up of in the first picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1523 is, I think, the same again, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, that's another body, in fact. That's the bottom of the stairs. The previous picture was the top of the stairs, and there was another -- there was a body here and then a body at the top, and then there were bodies in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And simply for completeness, because we've done all photographs bar one of this small album, on a separate topic, the very last photograph, 2690, shows what of significance?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: One of the main HVO force multipliers, if you like. It's a four-barrelled anti-aircraft gun mounted on a flatbed lorry which was used as a fast support weapon to support infantry attacks or to simply shoot up villages and houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of efficiency did this weapon have?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was awesome. It's a 423-millimetre, I think they were, anti-aircraft cannon with a very high rate of fire, and when used in the ground role, they were devastating. They certainly would have destroyed our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Including your Warriors? They would have destroyed your Warriors?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, can you remember when this photograph was taken and where?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I can't. I have a clear recollection of that vehicle and vehicles similar to it in and around the area of Vitez and Busovaca during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to complete this, the uniforms that you can see here, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, they are HVO uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come back to sweep up one or two outstanding questions, but only a few, I want you to help us again with the map. So if you could go to the map, and if the technical department could get as good a picture of the map as a whole, I would be very grateful. Colonel, if you would remember again that although the map will be available for the Chamber in either this form or, if they desire it, in some reduced form, it's necessary to spell out the towns because they obviously can't be read on the television screen or from the distance that the Chamber is from you. Did the attacks of which you became aware initially make any military sense?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In the morning of the 16th and early into the 17th, they didn't appear to make any military sense, other than the fact they were coordinated. It was as time passed, especially after my discussions at the conference on the 21st with General Halilovic and General Petkovic, that the form and the need for the coordination of the offensive began to explain itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us then first with what routes there were to Croatia for areas that were Croat-dominated in this part of Bosnia? Your Honours, I'm not sure actually how well the marking shows up, but I hope it's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Right. We're talking really about the main centres of Kiseljak, Busovaca, and Vitez, and with the small villages in the environs, including Fojnica here. The traditional road south into Croatia proper was down to Mostar. This road was completely dominated by the Serbs, who had taken positions on the high ground and were able to control the roads with mortars and artillery and essentially deny that for use as what we would describe as an MSR. The main route that was used was the same as we used, because we also got shelled and bombed by the Serbs trying to go down the main road, and that was I think we called it Route Triangle, I can't recall it's exact name, and that essentially went up to this junction here just short of Travnik and down this road system here to Gornji Vakuf, down into Prozor and down into Tomislavgrad and into Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I ask the witness, apart from the element of time, the attacks starting about the same time, was there any other factor that indicated that the attacks were coordinated?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The use of heavy artillery, which was not a resource that the village-level commanders would ordinarily be able to get to support their sort of military attacks. If -- in isolated inter-village inter-brigade disagreements that resulted in fighting, there was very rarely used large-calibre indirect fire weapons such as heavy mortars and artillery. And on this morning, the propensity of heavy artillery and heavy mortars led us to believe that it was coordinated and driven from a high level of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the artillery pieces would have to have been put in place in advance?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And allocated in advance?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: And supplied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In addition to the route you've already pointed out leading down to Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, were there other routes leading to other places, in particular down to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In the week or so preceding, Major Rule, who commanded B Company in Gornji Vakuf, had been tasked to find out what the fighting was reported by the UNHCR in the villages to the east of Prozor, here (indicating). And we couldn't initially understand why there was fighting in what had been ordinarily a very quiet area, and certainly, given the size of the Croat population of Prozor and the relative tiny size of the minority Muslim population in these villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: -- that it could only be a Croat agenda. It couldn't be a Muslim agenda, because if they tried to do anything, they would be destroyed. Major Rule was unable to get into these villages because a very large force, including tanks, denied his access and refused to allow him. He came back and said unless he received authority to fight his way through, then he wouldn't be able to get through. We spoke with our headquarters, and it was decided at that time that there was very little to be gained by actually launching a formal attack on the Croats. In subsequent analysis, and ongoing analysis during that week and into the week following the 16th, we deduced that it was actually the route that led up to Fojnica from Prozor that the Croats were actually trying to dominate, by removing the Muslim villages that were across this road. And although the road petered out to poor tracks in this area here, there was nevertheless a viable route linking Fojnica, Kakanj, and up to Busovaca, and therefore Vitez and Kiseljak, with Prozor. There was a bottleneck here (indicating) of Muslim villages that prevented unimpeded access for the Croat forces from Prozor to the Lasva Valley without using what was also a bottleneck in Gornji Vakuf, because Gornji Vakuf was a very mixed community, which had had considerable fighting in the previous month, and the fighting essentially was for control of the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So up to -- what, two routes into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Having the Serbs denied the main route, there were the possibility of two routes: one down through Gornji Vakuf, which presented a problem with the bottleneck here, and one down through Fojnica, which presented a problem with the bottleneck here, and it was at both those bottlenecks where the Croats were fighting. The routes up here were secured and largely in Croat hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come, then, to any comprehensible military objective in what happened at Ahmici and thereabouts, can you explain the other markings on the map? First of all, the green markings, which are just about visible as photographed.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The green lines are those that we had deduced and were shown to me by Mr. Merdan and General Petkovic as the axes of the BiH counterattack from the 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, of -- sorry; about 18, 19, 20 of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The red markings, some of them being lines, some of them being lines with arrows?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They are the -- the areas of fighting in the Kiseljak Valley, the area around Kakanj, and out of Vitez into Stari Vitez, Kruscica, along the Lasva Valley, clearing the main road between Vitez and Busovaca, and also up at -- I can't remember its name -- Pucarevo. And also in Pucarevo. So these were the -- as the morning of the 16th dawned, as we marked up our maps showing the fighting, these red areas showed where the fighting was on the morning of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the routes that you've identified had what political or military significance?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: With the onset of canton 10 and the establishing of a largely Croat canton and area, it was in danger of being isolated, in the west by the largely Muslim population of Travnik, in the north by the very large concentration of Muslims in Zenica, and the small but vociferous Muslim communities along the Kiseljak Valley. And equally, the community in Stari Vitez and on the villages along the main Lasva Valley, which dominated the road, they all had the ability to cut the road and isolate the Croat community within -- within the Lasva Valley. And so, essentially, they would be surrounded and not have vehicular access out of their canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The need to give access for that canton to Croatia proper being ... ?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, for it to have any form of sustainable political and military cohesiveness, it would have to have the means to resupply itself without being at the beck and call of the Muslim community. If they didn't have a secure route from Central Bosnia down to Croatia, then, really, it wasn't sustainable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just deal in detail with the checkpoint in Kacuni, if you can.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Kacuni, here (indicating). There had always been a checkpoint at Kacuni, which was a strategic junction with the Kiseljak road and the road leading to the main dual carriageway through Zenica, as there was a checkpoint in Vitez and as there was a checkpoint in Novi Travnik, I think this generic area was called, and each of those checkpoints were fundamental to the securing of the route. And the routes -- and the significance of the routes in a mountainous country is stark and obvious, because you can't take any viable group of people or vehicles over the mountains. You've got to use the routes, and the routes tend to be in the valleys, and so these routes were of strategic significance. And the way that the Bosnian people controlled their routes was by placing checkpoints on them, especially at the beginning and end of major towns and villages. These checkpoints were of tactical and strategic significance, and it was the fall of the checkpoint, following the BiH offensive, that essentially signalled to Colonel Blaskic that he had lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's pick up that point. You spoke of the ceasefire negotiation, the last one, being conducted in circumstances where Kordic was at risk of being surrounded, or was surrounded. Can you just point that out to the Chamber on the map a little more graphically?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah. Essentially, the main three axes of the 3rd Corps counterattack came down here and essentially captured just the high ground above Dubravica, therefore cutting the road here (indicating), to Vitez, and dominating Vitez. They came down here (indicating) and cut the road at the strategic junction here (indicating), and they forced a group around to relieve Kruscica through Kakanj and cut the road down to Fojnica from Busovaca. And so, essentially, all the routes out of Busovaca, either down to Kiseljak, Fojnica, Vitez, were essentially cut, and so the people and garrison in Busovaca couldn't be resupplied, couldn't be reinforced, and couldn't evacuate their casualties. And so, essentially, they were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If one looks at the map, Ahmici is not necessarily distinguishable from other villages along the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, closer to the microphone, Mr. Nice, please. Could you come closer to the microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a request from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm very sorry. I'll come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ahmici, on the map, might look much like many other villages. Did it in fact have any particular significance? How does it fit as a military target, or otherwise, on this particular morning?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It had two significances that we established. The first was its position on the main road that leads along the Lasva Valley and the ability of it to influence that road; and secondly, and a slightly more esoteric significance, was it was essentially a centre of Muslim culture within that part of Central Bosnia and produced, for example, a disproportionate number of imams than other villages of comparable size. So within the psyche and culture of the Muslim people of Central Bosnia, Ahmici had a very special significance. And so by destroying Ahmici, not only do you achieve the objective of securing the road, but you also hope to destroy the morale, break the will, maybe, of the people of Central Bosnia, the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Would you like to take your seat again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be, in the previous trial, the marked map was reduced to a map of this size, which can act as an aide-memoire because you can see the colours on it, but you can barely see the villages. If the Chamber lets me know what, if any, version of this map it would like other than the original, I'll endeavour to have the appropriate size printed for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel, just a couple of outstanding issues. As a final -- it's paragraph 6 of the summary -- you've dealt with the strategic value of the lines of communication. As to the populations or the inhabitants of the various places attacked, what was the purpose being served by the attack?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The purpose being served was to remove, in our judgement and my judgement, was to remove the minority Muslim population from canton 10, and so -- especially on the fringes of it, and in so doing, secure it, and most importantly also secure the routes within canton 10 linking the major centres of Croat population, and also provide a main supply route or a road link out of canton 10 down to Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've now dealt, I think, with the whole history, bringing us to this point in April. Were there any later contacts you had with Blaskic or Kordic? Or was that it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I didn't speak to Mr. Kordic again, and I had various meetings with Colonel Blaskic right up until the day I left Vitez in May, dealing with ceasefire violations and generally re-establishing a regime and the facilitating of the movement of aid within that part of Bosnia, very much moving back to the original mission statement we had, as opposed to embroiling ourselves in the conflict, which we had done for the previous six weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did any of those encounters with Blaskic, or any other experiences, displace the judgement you'd formed about the command structures within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not at all. The only thing that I formed an opinion of, and it was not -- it couldn't be attributed to a specific sentence or phrase, was that the relationship between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic had cooled somewhat and that Colonel Kordic had allegedly accused Colonel Blaskic of failing in his military mission and endangering the lives of the people of Busovaca. We encountered a slight frostiness or division within the relationship between those two particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had, of course, now had the experience of the ceasefire negotiation where Kordic was not present but you sought assurances from Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your view of the dual chain of command remained?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what did you liken it, if anything, from other experience or knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, one couldn't help -- and without wanting to make sort of an hysterical statement, but given the very close similarities between the Croatian and German culture, and the similarities between the Croatian army and the German army, and their relationships in the Second World War, you couldn't help but look at the structure of the HVO in many ways as the German army had been structured during the Second World War, and that the sort of paramilitary element of the army appeared to follow the political chain of command, where the political chain of command appeared to have specific military units dressed differently and more efficient-looking units to implement, if you like, strategic decisions, whereas the majority of the army were implementing the overall mission. And certainly in Central Bosnia it appeared that Mr. Kordic exercised control of these military/paramilitary forces, and Colonel Blaskic exercised control over the more conventional military forces. And on occasion, they came into conflict -- I don't mean physical conflict; I mean disagreement -- as to the primacy of particular tasks and missions on any given occasion. And I had very little -- from my personal experience and understanding, I had very little faith, as time went on, that we could guarantee to have something delivered on the ground without it being directed from Mostar, to ensure that the political chain of command was also following the party line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other matter that I haven't covered on the summary, and indeed I haven't asked you about before, so deal with these questions, please, just cautiously and with a "yes/no" approach wherever possible. Was there any information coming to you to the effect that perpetrators of the Ahmici massacre had been named by anyone? Just "Yes" or "No" to that.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without giving names, that's what I at present want to avoid, tell us what it was you learnt of the naming of them.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: A list of names had been given to BritBat, and that list of names, which I saw, was held by Colonel Stewart, and he confronted Colonel Blaskic with that list of names and asked him what he was going to do about it. It was a great source of dismay to Colonel Stewart, who quite admired Colonel Blaskic on a professional basis, that he at that point appeared to do nothing about it and contravened the rules of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So those names were made available, they were put in to the Croat chain of command?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many names were there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I can't remember; I think there were about 11, but I could be wrong. It was something that was dealt with -- it was very sensitive, and the source of the names was very sensitive, and it was dealt largely with by Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wanted to have a clarification on two matters from the witness. First, he has identified two chains of command, a military and a political; his assessment as to the chain that Mr. Kordic would fall under. And secondly, he said that in his view, Mr. Kordic exercised control over paramilitary units. If he could give an example of those units.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The first question, sir, was Mr. Kordic exercised control over the political chain of command; and the example of the hijacking of the convoy outside Busovaca and our need to negotiate directly with Mr. Kordic through our headquarters in Kiseljak and the HVO headquarters in Mostar and get Colonel Petkovic to give him a personal order, to Mr. Kordic, because Colonel Blaskic was unable to exercise authority over that situation. The defence, itself, of Busovaca, and the increasing military role in the defence of Busovaca, that Mr. Kordic took during the fighting between the 16th and the 21st led to my and our judgement that he had a military/paramilitary role. He wore a uniform, carried a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, my name is Steve Sayers. I represent Dario Kordic. I'm going to ask you a series of questions, and this is a rather artificial environment in some ways. You tend to speak very quickly, and the interpreters don't like that, and I'm the most notorious offender of that rule. I speak very quickly, too. So I would really appreciate it if you would pause a little bit between my question, think about your answer, then give your answer, and that would give the interpreters an opportunity to interpret.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The problem is that we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, your testimony concerns your experiences during a 93-day sojourn in Central Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I've never added up the days, but that sounds about right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You arrived in Central Bosnia on February the 6th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you left on May the 10th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you actually acceded to the position of Lieutenant Colonel Stewart's second in command, I believe, on February the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as of February the 20th, Colonel Stewart was your commanding officer, I take it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you speak Croatian, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, you functioned as Colonel Stewart's chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And your duties were to control the operational branches within your battalion headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Informational branches, too?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would say to coordinate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I understand it, there were three companies in your regiment: Alpha Company, based in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Bravo Company, based in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Charlie Company, based in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: We moved them around, but at the time of the 16th of April, that was the disposition. In addition, we had a Royal Engineers squadron and a reconnaissance squadron of the 9th 12th Lancers. So they were two further manoeuvre units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those manoeuvre units fell under your command as well?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Stewart's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you were in command when Colonel Stewart was not located at battalion headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the centre of your operations was in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The centre of operations was in Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's a relatively small town, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It is very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, its population is something in the range of seven to eight thousand, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'll take your word for that. It certainly isn't much bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the base that your battalion occupied was actually in the even smaller hamlet, if you like, of Nova Bila, somewhat to the north and west of Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are familiar with giving testimony in the cases that arise out of the events in the Lasva Valley in April of 1993, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: This is the third time I've given evidence, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. You testified for two days in the Blaskic case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was on November the 10th, 1997, and the next day?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then you testified for two days in the Kupreskic case, on August the 17th, 1998, and on the next day?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you were the first witness to testify in the Kupreskic case, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't suppose the witness knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He may not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also gave a short statement to the Prosecution investigators on September the 1st, 1994; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I do remember talking, sir. I couldn't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember giving the statement then?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you remember reviewing it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the name "Kordic" doesn't appear anywhere in that three-page statement?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't actually recall. I wouldn't be surprised if it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then you gave another much more detailed statement to the Prosecution on April the 16th, 1997, which is four years after you left your area of operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was 23 pages, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'll take your word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You reviewed those statements in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I've reviewed an abridged version of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Inaudible] -- the version for you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution counsel showed me a six-page statement last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that a statement that you had prepared or they had prepared for you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They had prepared it. I went through it and amended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I see. Did you review your testimony in the Blaskic and the Kupreskic cases in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, sir. I arrived last night, and I hadn't had time to come on an earlier visit to review any of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Reviewing that six-page document that was put together by the Prosecution for you, did that help you refresh your recollection as to certain events connected with your tour of duty through Central Bosnia six years ago?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you joined the British army, I believe, in 1972.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Essentially, you've been with the 1st Cheshire Regiment ever since?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I've done my what we would describe as regimental tours with my regiment, the Cheshire Regiment, and have done a series of other appointments on the staff or in training establishments away from my regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many soldiers are actually in your regiment?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It fluctuates, depending on the role that we are doing and how well recruited we are. The establishment for a Warrior battalion, which is what we were in Vitez, is 612 soldiers and about 35 officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But at the regimental level, how many soldiers are there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That is the regimental level. That doesn't include the attachments of engineers, lance -- the reconnaissance, or other administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there under the command of the Cheshire Battalion in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In the region of about 800, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you actually took command of the regiment in 1996.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've essentially been in the army, and you're a professional military man, for the last 26 years?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You anticipate spending the rest of your professional career in the army?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: If they'll continue to employ me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Would it be fair to say that you've been all around the globe during your two and a half decades in the British army, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I've served in a lot of countries, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is true that you have spent your entire professional life as a soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You don't have any political training, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Other than that training that we give our officer core in defence and international affairs, which is a thread of training that runs through our professional education.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But that's it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you had, I believe, a range of military information and intelligence documentation and resources available to you.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those, at least some of them, were prepared contemporaneously with the events that occurred certainly in Central Bosnia, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was there any marked departure from the regularity of preparation of those sorts of documents in your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, as opposed to other tours of duty that you have been on in the world?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I had not before served as a member of the United Nations, and the procedures and documentation that is done within the United Nations differs from other things I've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the information resources available to you would have included, for example, military information summaries, or milinfosums, as they are popularly known; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. They were actually prepared by our own milinfo cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was headed by Captain Chris Leyshon; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and that was Sergeant Major Connelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Those are daily correlations of the most significant information available to your various intelligence-gathering arms in the battalion, and they are prepared day by day?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Information gathering, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your view, are those military information summaries generally accurate?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: What they represent each day is an assessment of the events of the day, set in context of as what has happened before, and depending on the availability of people to agree them, the judgement either of the commanding officer, myself, Captain Leyshon, or Sergeant Major Connelly as to the interpretation of those events. So any one taken in isolation represented on that day our views and opinions and information. The next day, we may well contradict, as we receive further data, what we say the day before. So I don't think you can ever say that on a day, they are accurate. But as time went on, they became more informed and more representative, possibly, of the reality. But they still represented an information summary as opposed to fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So they may or may not be accurate --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- on a particular day?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you have available to you a battalion war diary?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed that document?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does that document contain any reference to the dual lines of command that you've theorised existed in Central Bosnia, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't remember. The war diary was maintained largely by the adjutant, and it is not a necessarily authoritative document. I would rely more on the milinfosums and the daily situation reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the daily situation reports, sir, could you just tell the Trial Chamber what those might be?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They were prepared by the operational centre of the battalion and essentially dealt in the facts as reported into the operation cell from the various companies and would be a summary of those, with an interpretation either by the commanding officer or myself at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was it that directed tanks and ambulances into the village of Ahmici at about 11.00 a.m. on April the 16th, 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In overall terms, probably myself, and in the detail, I think it was OCA Company, Major now Colonel Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. There isn't any doubt, actually, that your battalion's tanks and ambulances were in the village of Ahmici at about 11.00 a.m. on the 16th of April, 1993, is there, Colonel Watters?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There is no doubt at all that they were in parts of the village of Ahmici, but you would have to understand the geography of Ahmici to understand that you can be in parts of it and not see other parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, the question was, sir, that you had armed and armoured vehicles in Ahmici on the 16th of April at about 11.00 a.m. Did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, radio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, if you're moving on to another topic, it's now 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will move to courtroom II this afternoon. Perhaps someone could direct the witness there. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Sayers resumes, the Court's been reconstructed with the map on view, but the English booth has expressed their disquiet because they can see nothing; apart from any claustrophobia that that may instil, they also find it much more difficult to do their job without the advantage of seeing the people, by and large, who are speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are there any questions, Mr. Sayers, about that map in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only question that I would have, I think, Your Honour, would be just to get the witness to reaffirm that that green circle that he's put on there, or someone put on there, represents the encirclement of Croat forces by the forces of the 3rd Corps on -- I believe he said April the -- between April the 19th and April the 20th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, as I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Other than that, I don't think I would have any other questions, with maybe one exception, and that would be with respect to the village of Kacuni that you've talked about, Colonel Watters, could you just indicate where that is on the map for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Kacuni (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the village of Bilalovac, please. It should be just a kilometre or so southeast of that.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: (indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's take the map down. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before the lunch break, Colonel Watters, we were just discussing the sources of intelligence and information available to you and your colleagues. You had mentioned daily situation reports. Do you know whether there were any daily situation reports maintained by your battalion between April the 15th, 1993, and April the 21st, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There would have been one each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So those should still be available, I take it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In existence?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: They should be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those daily situation reports would reflect the reports that were being received from the various British Battalion call signs who were driving around the Lasva Valley and its environs during those dates?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It would be a synopsis of them. It wouldn't give the detail of each report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, your battalion also kept routine radio logs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And have you consulted those radio logs to determine whether there is any reference at all to the conversation that you described to the Trial Chamber with some unidentified person who supposedly spoke to one of the soldiers in your battalion, who supposedly spoke with an HVO unidentified person, and the name of Mr. Kordic was mentioned in connection with the apprehension of a convoy?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that the kind of document or is that the kind of event that would be recorded in a radio log, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's a very difficult question to answer, because the radio log is maintained at battalion level by a lieutenant or captain and at company level, which is where the detail of the conversation would take place, by a private or lance corporal. And it would really depend on the amount of other things that were going on, and so -- he should do; whether he does or not, I couldn't say. I don't know if that radio log exists, and I don't know today the location of the majority of those radio logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that the only evidence that we have is your recollection of that conversation six years ago?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and the fact that I had to deal through Kiseljak to Mostar to get Mr. Kordic to agree to release the convoy, which supports my memory that he was the focus for the taking of that convoy that we had to release.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, who did you speak to at Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I didn't personally speak to Mostar. I spoke to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who at Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I would have spoken to the operations desk, and I have a memory of speaking to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Brigadier Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who did he speak to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I believe he or his representatives spoke to Mostar, spoke to General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it Brigadier Cordy-Simpson, or one of his representatives?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You weren't there at that conversation, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I was using a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to whom they spoke?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And similarly, you have no idea who was contacted -- who contacted whom following that call that may or may not have occurred to Mostar, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The call did occur, sir. I can't tell you who made it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know who they called, and you don't know who that person called in Busovaca or Vitez or wherever, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I don't follow your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you don't know who received the call from Mostar relating to the release of this convoy, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect to, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You certainly don't know whether any call was made to Mr. Kordic in that regard, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was -- I was told by Kiseljak that Mr. Kordic had been told by Mostar to release the convoy, and the convoy was released. That was the beginning and end of my interest in it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But my question to you, Colonel Watters, was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's fairly obvious that -- the witness has given his evidence, and he doesn't say that he was present at any of this. He is describing what he has heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, just turning your attention back to February of 1993, Colonel Watters, you had stated that when you arrived in Central Bosnia, your biggest challenge, to use your words, was to get a clear understanding of Balkan history; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so much Balkan history. Certainly, what was happening at the time and what had led up to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You needed to get an understanding of the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Specifically in our area of responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in the State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not in the State of Croatia, as such. I was interested in the British area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You wanted to obtain an understanding of the current aspirations of the Serbs, the Muslims, --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and the Croats within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Throughout the former Yugoslavia, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That would probably be quite an arrogant thing to try and -- say I was trying to do. I was immediately concerned with what was going on in the area for which I was about to be the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You spent, I believe, 48 hours doing that.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No. I spent, I think you said, 93 days doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, do you remember sending a statement -- actually, an amended witness statement, through your captain, Captain Dutton, on the 16th of April, 1997, to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I remember sending several things, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember saying the following, on pages 2 to 3: "When I first arrived, my biggest challenge was to get a clear understanding of Balkan history and the current situation in BiH, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. I also wanted to understand, as far as I could from the available reference material, the current aspirations of the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats within our own area of responsibility and throughout the former Yugoslavia. I spent 48 hours doing that"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. In general terms, the wider picture. In other words, I had not actually been aware of what was happening in the former Yugoslavia until I arrived there, and so I had a steep learning curve to understand, first of all, where in Europe I was, what had been going on there, and what our role was in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that shortly after your arrival, perhaps within a week, you attended a meeting of the Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That meeting was held in the town of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall who the European Monitoring Mission representative was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of Jeremy Fleming?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Fleming, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was the chairman of the commission, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sitting on the commission were not only Mr. Fleming but your C.O., Colonel Stewart; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not on that day, no, because he was on R & R.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were there as his representative, I take it.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I was there. The then second in command, Major Tim Park, was there as his representative. I was merely there as an observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. In addition, I believe that Colonel Blaskic, from the Central Bosnia Operation Zone of the HVO, sat on that commission.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Along with his deputy, Colonel Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The other representatives on the BiH side were General Enver Hadzihasanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Also his second in command, Colonel Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic never sat on that commission, did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He wasn't involved in any way with the Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission at any time throughout its existence, to your knowledge, was he?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Central Bosnia, would it be fair to say and accurate to say that you arrived in a situation of the utmost military, political, and ethnic confusion, if you like, in the middle of a civil war?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I certainly found it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Everyone was fighting everyone, the Serbs fighting the Muslims and the Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Muslims and the Croats fighting the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Occasionally, the Muslims and the Croats fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, before you arrived in the theatre, that approximately a week and a half before your arrival, there had been a massacre of Croat civilians in the villages of Dusina, Lasva, Nezirovici, Gusti Grab, and other villages?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not first-hand, obviously, because it was before my arrival. I was aware that there had been accusations of massacres all over Central Bosnia. I didn't focus on any particular ones.
