utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know where Dusina is and Lasva?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I probably did. Today, I would have to study the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, to the best of your recollection, they are about five kilometres northeast of Busovaca, both of those small villages?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute about that. Would it be fair to say that Gusti Grab is a village that is adjacent to one of the villages that you pointed out to the Trial Chamber, Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember the specific name of every hamlet and village, but I'm sure it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Also would it be fair to say that the United Nations actually controlled the checkpoint at Kacuni at the time of your arrival in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that throughout your time in the theatre, Colonel Watters, the stretch of the main supply route, the MSR, I believe you called it, from Kacuni to Bilalovac was controlled by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair comment, I think, for virtually all of the time. I can't actually say, during the period 16th to 18th, exactly what was going on down there, but for the majority of time there were Muslim checkpoints on that part of the road. Certainly every time I travelled that road, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. That basically cut the communications, from the Croat perspective, anyway, --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- throughout the time that you were in the theatre; right? In other words, there was no communication between, for example, the town of Busovaca and the town of Kiseljak further to the south?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Because part of the reason for us being there and putting checkpoints was to facilitate the free movement of people up and down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, humanitarian convoys; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, the free passage and safety of all up and down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're saying that Croats were free to travel, at least from your perspective, I gather, from Vitez to the Kaonik junction, and then south through Busovaca to Kiseljak, without interference or obstruction by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Certainly to Busovaca. From Busovaca to Kiseljak, there was always the problem of interference because of the Muslim checkpoints on the road, and that's why we were asked by Colonel Blaskic and the Busovaca commission to place checkpoints ourselves on that road, to give security and confidence to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see any of the joint orders that were signed by Croat forces and Muslim forces at the Kakanj/Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission meeting on February the 13th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic did not sign any of those documents at all, did he?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, he wasn't involved for a second in the negotiation of any of those documents or orders, was he?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: As you said before, he wasn't at the meeting, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those orders dealt with things such as, for example, the withdrawal of troops; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the return of people to their homes; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the release of detainees?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the removal of checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the filling in of trenches and bunkers?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And with the resolution of incidents that might occur in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The name of the commission is a slight misnomer. It was named because it was accommodated in Busovaca. It was responsible for the area of Central Bosnia, and at that time its main focus was the then disputes along the Kiseljak Valley road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, the commission actually changed its seat, if you like, from Busovaca in January and February of 1993 to the BritBat base at Nova Bila, just outside of Vitez, in March of 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the commission that resolved incidents in the Vitez/Busovaca area, from March of 1993 until the end of your tour, operated in Vitez, essentially?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir, and became marginally less effective as the troubles developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand your testimony, your battalion's area of responsibility stretched from Kiseljak through Busovaca, up to Zenica, then along the Lasva Valley through Vitez to Travnik, and actually as far as Maglaj to the north and Jajce to the west.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I think Jajce was actually behind the Serb lines, but in that direction, yes, and then north to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The principal mission statement that you had while you were in Central Bosnia was to facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid through your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've also referred to some sort of implied, I believe was your word, mission statement, which was to stop the loss of life?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That was an implied task of the mission, sir, yes. I think to prevent loss of life is how we phrased it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To prevent loss of life. You would certainly agree with me, would you not, that BritBat had, to use your words, the combat power to achieve that mission statement?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't support that, sir, because we singularly failed, for a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I say I wouldn't support that because we failed to prevent the loss of life. We didn't have the combat power. What we did have was considerably greater combat power than any of the other Bats at the time in UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know Lieutenant Colonel Alistair Duncan?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I haven't seen him for a number of years. He's now a brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier Duncan told Jane's Defence Weekly, in October of 1995, that during his sojourn in Central Bosnia, he was the most powerful man in Central Bosnia, with 50 Warrior infantry fighting vehicles. He was actually Colonel Stewart's immediate replacement, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: His battalion replaced our battalion, and he was the commander of Op Grapple 2, which was the successor to our operation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Along the lines of what he said, I believe that your battalion actually had 53 Warrior armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I think we had about 51 when we left, because we had several blown up by mines. But, yes, that was approximately our figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You had other armoured vehicles --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- such as Scimitars?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What is a Warrior? Could you just tell the Trial Chamber what this vehicle looks like? Is it armed, and if so, with what?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: A Warrior is a 30-ton armoured fighting vehicle. It consists of a chamber, which is protected by armour, in which sit eight infantry soldiers, and on top of it is a turret which has a 30-millimetre cannon and a coaxially-mounted machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's a Hughes 7,62-millimetre chain gun; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It has an extremely high, rapid rate of fire?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It's a very efficient machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The 30-millimetre Radan cannon with which the Warrior is equipped fires high-explosive shells and has a range of up to 2.000 metres, I believe.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It fires a variety of ammunition at a variety of ranges, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What's the maximum range of the weapon, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Depending on which ammunition you select to use, around a thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How do you aim this weapon?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Through an optical sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A telescopic sight?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Scimitar vehicles that your battalion deployed in Central Bosnia were also equipped with a 30-millimetre, high-velocity cannon as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you said you had something in the order of 800 soldiers at your disposal in Central Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and that you had combat power, as you've just described, that others did not possess?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more general questions before we start hitting specific areas, Colonel Watters. Would it be fair to say that the social, political, and military situation that confronted you during your three months in the area from February until May of 1993 was a situation of complete anarchy and chaos?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- in actual literal interpretation of those words, I wouldn't agree. There was a degree of anarchy and there was a degree of chaos. After the Serb offensive stopped in November, December, there was a degree of order established within our area of responsibility, and we were able, with the support of the BiH and the HVO, to facilitate the movement of aid throughout our TOR. So I think to say "anarchy" and "chaos" is probably exaggerating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, there was a huge crime wave that was cresting throughout your area of responsibility during your tour through Central Bosnia; wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There was certainly lawlessness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, that crime wave overarched everything that you'd been dealing with, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: You would have to explain what you mean by that. I mean, it didn't interfere with us doing our business; it just added to the work we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, do you remember testifying in the Blaskic case two years ago, at page 3382, lines 21 through 24: "There was a great deal of crime going on throughout the area. It overarched everything we had been doing because dealing with criminal activity, thefts of vehicles, robberies, and so on."

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: But you were talking about anarchy and chaos. There was a crime wave, and it often deflected us from what we were there to do. The point I'm making is it didn't -- although it made our lives more complicated, it didn't prevent us also doing what we were there to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you found the military situation, and the environment generally, upon your arrival -- I think you would agree with this -- very confusing and difficult to understand?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know when the civil war actually broke out?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: In Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: About six months before the U.N. deployed, so we're probably talking -- in the immediate area, I think it was about -- beginning of '92; somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was actually founded on the 6th of March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I probably did then, sir, but I -- I have to admit I haven't kept that sort of information in my brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree that the city of Mostar was surrounded by Serb and JNA forces on March the 16th, 1992, just ten days after the republic had been founded?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I have a memory of being briefed to that effect. I need to just explain that I was living in Borneo at the time, and we didn't have television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you also agree that one month later, in April of 1992, the capital of the country, Sarajevo, was completely surrounded and cut off by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: By "Serb forces," I mean people of Serb ethnicity from Bosnia-Herzegovina; not people from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, sir. In fact, I visited Sarajevo a couple of times, and there were still Serb checkpoints governing the routes in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So that by the time you arrived in Vitez on February the 6th, the country had been independent for eleven months and at a state of civil war for about ten months and twenty days?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That would seem right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you know that the Armija of Bosnia and Herzegovina had issued general mobilisation orders in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I was aware of it, yes, sir. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's just a few weeks before you arrived, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact, all of the local Muslims in the Vitez area were receiving call-up orders by January the 13th, 1993, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we had information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall reading that information in milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that was accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, people were being called up, yes, but they were being called up everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me just show you, if I may, a document, and ask you whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D57/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just take a few minutes, Colonel Watters, and just tell us whether you recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall when you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was in April, I think, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be -- would it refresh your recollection for me to suggest that it was written on April the 7th, 1993, approximately nine days or eight days before the events that you've principally testified about today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What led to you write this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I hadn't communicated with my father and various other people, and so I wrote a sort of standard letter to them to tell them what I was doing and what was going on where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What did you need to clear your conscience for, as you stated in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That I hadn't written to people. My conscience was that I hadn't written to my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when you wrote the observations that are contained in this document, sir, did you -- these were sentiments expressed from your heart, if you were --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- if you like?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if you take a look on the second page, you make the observation about halfway down in the -- or just more than -- a little more than halfway down in the first paragraph, "We have pushed our mandate to its limit. We have, for example, transported displaced military units whose existence was upsetting the delicate Croat/Muslim local ethnic balance"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You previously described to the Trial Chamber a contention that was made by Colonel Blaskic relating to BritBat supposedly transporting Muslim units as a contention that was, to use your words, I believe, "patently ridiculous"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you actually transport Muslim military units?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The innuendo from Colonel Blaskic that we were moving these people -- or the actual specific allegation was that we were moving these people within our Warrior vehicles. The actual convoy I'm talking about here was a convoy of about 15 buses that Captain Sherlock, second in command of A Company, escorted from Gornji Vakuf to, I think, Zenica, I think in February or March, at the request of the HVO, because this brigade -- which I think was called the Jajce Brigade -- after the fall of Jajce had moved into the area of Gornji Vakuf and had upset the status quo, and we were asked, as part of our ceasefire negotiation in Gornji Vakuf, to assist with the moving of this brigade from Gornji Vakuf out of that area and into another area, which is what we agreed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So what Colonel Blaskic was saying actually was not patently ridiculous, was it, at all? It was true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, it was patently ridiculous, because it was the HVO that had asked us to move the Jajce Brigade, which was a Muslim Brigade. The accusation Colonel Blaskic was making was that during the fighting, from the 16th to 20th of April, we were engaged in moving groups of Muslim soldiers inside our Warriors around the field of battle, which was patently ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've previously described, on the evening of the 16th of April, I believe, transporting some wounded men from the Muslim headquarters in Kruscica to a medical facility; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And those people were taken from the Muslim headquarters in Kruscica, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, they were taken from a house in Kruscica. They weren't taken from the headquarters. They were in the cellar of a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked to go pick up some injured women and children, I believe?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you found injured men instead?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you did transport them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, in our ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: And reported the fact to Colonel Blaskic, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is, please?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna: What is it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: A community of Croatians in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what it is? Does that name ring a bell at all?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see the point of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's a question which is being -- Mr. Sayers, this isn't some sort of test. What is the point of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, the point, Judge May, is that this gentleman and others--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And don't address me by my -- you should not address the Court by its name. You know the way to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. The point is this: Colonel Watters and other military officers have all testified that they took efforts to inform themselves of the military and political structure of the various communities which they had within their area of responsibility. Clearly the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was one of the most significant of the political communities within the area of responsibility of this soldier and other soldiers like him, and I think it's significant that he's hearing -- at least I think he is hearing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the expression "the community of Herceg-Bosna" mean anything to you? Now, Colonel Watters, you've heard that question. What would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid my memory is dulled by time. It evokes a memory of a very ideologically strong Croat Bosnian community that was establishing its right to existence within the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent cultural group; not as a sort of outstation of Croatia, but as actually ethnic peoples within themselves. That's -- I couldn't give you the actual thrust of it. That's my memory from six years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Colonel Watters, but your understanding was that this was a cultural organisation, essentially?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: When I say -- I said a culture, I mean, with its aspirations for self-determination, its own structure, its -- you know, its military capability, a peoples within the -- the peoples, the Catholic Croatian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether Mr. Kordic had any role or position or office within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: He was a vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've mentioned the name "Mate Boban" before; do you know whether Mr. Boban was the holder of any office within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a very senior member of that. I can't remember whether he was the president or a senior vice-president, I'm afraid. He only entered my area of interest on his visit to Travnik. I really didn't look too much at the political structure of Mostar because it was outside of our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know who was the head of the HVO government in Vitez when you were there, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The mayor of Vitez was an influential political figure in Vitez, and I would -- I would presume he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what his name was?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I did, and I can't remember. I met him on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As the Court has properly pointed out, this isn't a memory contest: Does the name Ivica Santic sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Santic, yeah, I think we used to pronounce it. I'm afraid our Bosnian pronunciation was not particularly good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what the name of the mayor of Busovaca was when you were there, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever met a gentleman by the name of Zoran Maric?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of meeting him. He might have been with a group of people I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you concentrated principally upon the military structures within your area of responsibility as opposed to the political structures?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That would be very fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know the name of the HVO military brigade that was stationed in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I did, and no, I can't remember the name of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can jog your memory, if I could ask the usher to show you Exhibit D49/1, please, and also Exhibit D50/1. I'm sorry; it was D51/1. D51/1. Turning your attention to Exhibit D49/1, do you recognise this as a copy of milinfosum 97 on the 6th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Without sounding pedantic, it looks like that is what it is. I can't say I remember it. I think this was just after I arrived, and I don't have a recollection of what each daily milinfosum looked like. But it's of the format that we produced, and I do remember reading on a milinfosum a summary of the command personalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you take a look at page 3, what was the name of the brigade -- well, does it jog your memory, in looking at this document, that it was the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade that was located in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: To be honest, the name doesn't actually leap into my consciousness; but if the milinfosum said that's what it was, then it would most likely have been accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with the commander of the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade, Niko Jozinovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't have a memory of meeting him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet the deputy commander, Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't remember him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you take a look at the next exhibit, it's another milinfosum, a little bit difficult to read, but on page 1, the commander of the Nikola Subic Zrjnski brigade on the 26th of February, 1992, appears to be Dusko Grubesic. Do you recall ever meeting with commander Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: His name is more familiar than the other ones you've given me but I don't have a specific memory of meeting him. May I explain something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The brigades is a slight misnomer in the nomenclature that I would use because they essentially were the village troops of that village, and some of the brigades were hundreds strong, some were in their 20s. And the responsibility within BritBat for liaising with the brigade commanders was bestowed on the liaison officers and the company commanders. I tended to focus with the commanding officer, at a slightly higher level and didn't involve myself in meeting and establishing personal relationships at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that you did not liaise regularly yourself with the military commanders in Busovaca itself?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That would be very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, your intelligence section, I believe was known as G2?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that your G2 section had accumulated, by the time that you left Central Bosnia in May of 1993, an enormous amount of intelligence relating to the chain of command of Croat, Muslim, and Serb forces in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Information, not intelligence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me. I'm sorry, Mr. Sayers; could we hear from the witness what is the distinction between intelligence and information? Would you please tell us, how would you define intelligence as opposed to information?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Intelligence is corroborated material on which one would base military decisions. Information is uncorroborated information that is used to form decisions, but you wouldn't necessarily make military judgements on it. In addition, as members of the United Nations, we had no remit to gather or process intelligence; we only had a remit to gather and process information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for elucidating that, Colonel Watters. In your view, therefore, there is an extremely sharp distinction between intelligence on the one hand and information on the other?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you use the term intelligence or information, you use it in a deliberate rather than an inadvertent way?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I try to, sir, as we all do. The slight problem is that our G2 cell is traditionally called an intelligence cell in the British army. On deployment to Bosnia we had to retitle it the information cell and it was very easy to slip back into the old nomenclature without actually meaning to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember giving an interview to the Prosecution on the 1st of September, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read to you from the second page there, quote: "The G2 (intelligence section) has an enormous amount of intelligence relating to the chain of command on both the Croatians, Muslim, and Serb structure. This information could be released with a formal request to the Ministry of Defence."

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah, I hold my hand up to mixing my nomenclature. I should have called it the information cell but at that time it was called the intelligence cell, because we were not in Bosnia. The intelligence I should have referred to as information, because that's what it was in Bosnia. I'm afraid we just really muddling nomenclature. It was not my remit to be able to release any of the material that we possessed. It would ultimately be the remit of the United Nations who would have to be approached, or our Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Do you ever recall seeing any organisational charts summarising the military organisation and chain of command of the HVO in Central Bosnia and which were prepared by your colleagues or yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll just show you, if I may, a document which I would like to have marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D58/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, Colonel Watters, have you taken a look at that document?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Never seen it before, I take it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then that need not detain us particularly long. Would it be fair to say that below the brigade level, you did not know what the chain of command or organisational structure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was a document that I thought, Your Honour, was prepared by BritBat. It was actually Exhibit 378 and 379 in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It hasn't been exhibited in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the moment we'll disregard it, because it's not been produced and this witness can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Returning to my question, Colonel Watters, would it be fair to say that below the brigade level, you did not know what the chain of command or organisational structure of the HVO was?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Personally, not in detail, unless I happened to focus on a particular brigade and ask to be briefed on what we knew about it, and we would endeavour through the liaison officers to understand the command structure within the brigades, although the liaison officer principally would focus on the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've referred to a detachment that was located in a building called the Bungalow in the village of Nadioci. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which brigade did that detachment belong to?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to the commander?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I think I did. I think it was the commander that was dealing with the situation on the 19th of April. At least he said he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he ever say that he reported only to Dario Kordic as opposed to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you just do not know to whom that person reported?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That -- other than he was HVO, and therefore I presume came under the command of Colonel Blaskic, that would be correct. I didn't know in detail who he reported to up his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And you never discovered any information or were told any information by anybody that led you to a contrary conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Only a supposition of coincidence. The description of those soldiers fitted the description of the soldiers who had hijacked the convoy whom we were told took their orders from Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But that was actually the only incident that you ever heard of that variety where the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- throughout your three months in Central Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the military organisation of the HVO, sir, if you had one?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was my understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was a region which had a series of operating areas, each with commanders, and under that were a series of brigades, and it was quite a formal structure with a clearly defined chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At the top of the clearly defined chain of command, would it be fair to say that an Operative Zone would be roughly equivalent to a battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, as -- that would be a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I would just like to get an idea of the numbers of soldiers that we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That was the problem we had. It was very difficult. The terms used, of brigades and operation zones and so on, were difficult for us, because the nomenclature of "brigade" in our terminology is a sort of minimum of three battle-group groupings, and so the numbers of what the British army would describe as a brigade didn't equate to what was described as a brigade in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many soldiers, if you know, were in the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't know. Whether I did know or not, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a widely variable number of soldiers within each brigade that was a member of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct; I mentioned that earlier. Some of them could be in their 20s and others could be in their hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to Colonel Blaskic, I believe that you first met him on February the 13th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was in Busovaca; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was at a meeting attended --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry, no, it wasn't in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I think I first met Colonel Blaskic in the French engineers' camp, at the meeting of the Busovaca Commission, was when I first met Colonel Blaskic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. That would have been in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that Colonel Blaskic's immediate commander was there too. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll just mention the name and see if that jogs your memory. Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting him at that meeting. I may have done, and if he was at the meeting, I probably would have done. I remember Colonel Blaskic. I don't remember General Petkovic, and my only clear recollection of meeting him was on the 21st of April. If you remember, I was essentially an observer of that meeting and so may well not have actually met him or been introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, throughout your acquaintance with Colonel Blaskic, there was absolutely no doubt in your mind that he was the overall commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, was there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, there was no doubt in my mind that that is what his title was and that was the authority he exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To you, he had all of the natural authority of the commander, did he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He reported directly to General Petkovic, in your experience, did he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He signed documents as regional commander of the HVO in your presence, did he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic never did, did he?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that Colonel Blaskic's headquarters was in the town of Vitez. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. He had another headquarters in Kiseljak, but the one that I met him in was in the school -- the hotel in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, Colonel Blaskic came from the Kiseljak region, did he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Blaskic initially said to you that it was the Serbs who had attacked Ahmici on April the 15th and 16th, 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You thought that that suggestion was ridiculous, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He also mentioned to you that if it wasn't the Serbs, it could have been the Muslims themselves that had attacked Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you think that that suggestion was ridiculous?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever read your commanding officer Colonel Stewart's book "Broken Lives"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read to you a short excerpt from it. He describes meeting Lieutenant Colonel Colm Doyle, who was a regular officer in the Irish army. He had just finished being Lord Carrington's special envoy, and I'm reading from page 29 to 30 of the book: "... and was shortly to return home after having spent the best part of a year in the region. He said that most people of Bosnia were very good at twisting the truth to suit their purposes. 'I never knew how much they can lie.' "He declared in his experience, all parties to the conflict were sometimes prepared to attack their own people, with the intention of placing the blame on others." Then on page 280 to 81, that theme is elaborated. "Colm Doyle, Lord Carrington's special assistant, had once told me that all sides in Bosnia were perfectly capable of killing their own for advantage." Did Colonel Stewart ever describe those conversations with Lieutenant Colonel Doyle to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and I also had conversations with Colonel Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he express the same views as those described in Colonel Stewart's book to you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? I mean is it being suggested that it was the Muslims who attacked Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that there is extremely considerable doubt as to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, listen, Mr. Sayers. It's not your thoughts that I want, it's your submissions which you must give to the Court. Now, if you are suggesting that this was a Muslim attack in which there were 96, I think it was, Muslim casualties, the evidence we heard the other day, and five Croat, then it's something which should be put to the witness in order that we can have his evidence upon it. Now, if you're going to suggest at any time to the Court that it was a Muslim attack upon Ahmici, you must put it to the witness that that was what happened. Are you going to make that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I can't make any suggestion one way or the other, Your Honour, because I don't know, and I don't believe the Defence knows who was responsible for the attack in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you are appearing in this case. At the end of the case, you are going to have to make submissions about what happened in Ahmici. Now, the Prosecution case on this is clear. It is that this was an attack by the HVO, which ended with the casualties in the way that we know is suggested. Now, if the Defence want to suggest something to the contrary, then it should be put to the witnesses who were there in order that they can deal with it. This witness has given evidence that, in his judgement, it was an attack by the HVO. Now, if you want to contradict that in due course, you must give him the opportunity of dealing with the case. Well, if it's suggested, Colonel Watters, that this was an attack by the Muslims or by the Serbs, what would your evidence about that be?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: From first-hand accounts of survivors who I spoke to after the incident, the reports of our soldiers who, during the day of the 16th, were evacuating casualties from the lower part of the village, and my observations of the general movement of troops around the area, I would say it's completely fanciful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so I can clear it up, Mr. President, our position is that there was fighting at Ahmici; that Ahmici, we believe, was defended not particularly heavily but defended nonetheless. In fact, I believe that some of the soldiers who were deployed in Ahmici on the morning of the 16th, namely, Lieutenant Dooley and Mr. Wooley, actually saw soldiers carrying AKM weapons on that day. So I think that our position is that the village was defended. There's no question that there was fighting there. Who started the fight, we just don't know. That's what this trial is all about, in some respects, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course you may not know, but you're going to have to adopt a position in order that the issues can be clarified. If the position is no more than, "We are not in a position to dispute what the Prosecution say about it," so be it. But at some stage, these matters are going to have to be clarified. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just turn to the observations that I made to the Court and just ask Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember, Colonel Watters, speaking with Lieutenant Dooley, following his deployment to Ahmici on the morning of the 16th, and being told that British troops had actually spotted armed Muslim troops carrying AKM weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There were BiH and HVO troops all over the Lasva Valley carrying weapons on that morning, and I had several conversations with Dooley and various other people. I cannot recollect, in all honesty, a specific conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall speaking with I think it was Sergeant Wooley, Matthew Robert Wooley?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I think he was a lieutenant in the 9th 12th Lancers. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I guess we'll take that up with Lieutenant Wooley. But he did say to the Prosecutors in February of 1997 that, "I wish to mention that I came across not more than ten combatants from the Muslim side. Four are seen in photographs," which we haven't seen. "Some of them are carrying AKMs. Some did not have any weapons at all." Do you remember him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I don't. Sorry, he saw them where?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't remember having that conversation with him. There were -- as I say, there were groups of people all over the place. It wouldn't surprise me that there were groups of armed Muslims in and around Ahmici and all the other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Sayers, I should like to ask a question of the witness to add something to what was explained by Mr. President to yourself. Just a moment ago, when you looked at the photographs, you told us that after the events in Ahmici, you went through the village with your men. You went there from one house to the other, and we saw the photographs which you identified. When you entered the village and saw those houses and saw what happened here and there, those photographs of the barn and so on and so forth, all that you saw, did it seem to you the effect or the aftermath of a normal battle between armed forces, conducted in a conventional combat? That is, did it seem to you the aftermath of a normal battle waged by some regular army soldiers? Did it look like the aftermath of a normal battle, conventional battle?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, Sir, it looked like the aftermath of a massacre, and the thing that was stark and most obvious was the -- the village of Ahmici is essentially two parts, the upper part of the village up the valley, which was the largely Muslim part, and the lower part, which was a little more mixed, and about halfway up the village were a line of Croat houses. Beyond the line of Croat houses, there wasn't a single building, of the 20 or 30 buildings, houses, that had not been totally destroyed, and there wasn't a single piece of damage done to the Croat houses. I banged on the door of one of the Croat houses because I could see they were in there. They wouldn't come out and talk to us, and at that point we were shot at from up above these houses, from the woods, and we then withdrew. In my judgement, if there had been resistance from those Bosnian Muslim soldiers who might have been in that village, they weren't able to resist very well, because their entire village was destroyed. Every house was burnt, and later we buried 96 people from the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Those persons whom you found in the village and whom you then buried, were they, to your mind, in your view, civilians? Were they civilians or military or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: The majority were women and old men, and there were some younger men who may well have been soldiers. But the vast majority of the bodies that I saw were civilians, but one could never -- because a body was in civilian clothes, one could not say it hadn't been a soldier. That's quite a technical point, Sir. But the vast majority of the people to me looked like civilians. There were a few younger men who could have been soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in your experience in this militarily- and politically-confused time that characterised your tour of duty through Central Bosnia, that all men of military age, between the ages of, say, 16 and 65, were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the vast majority. I wouldn't say up to 65. I can't remember the exact age. But whenever you came into a situation, it was very rare, in a civilian situation in the villages or towns, to find men of military age. They were mostly on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Occasionally, when they rotated back to their villages, they would bring their weapons with them, I take it.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That appeared to be the norm, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And whatever bits and pieces of uniform that they may have been able to accumulate over the past few months?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. They would normally be wearing a hat or a jacket or an arm band or something like that designating their particular military group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it also be fair to say that you found a huge variation in uniform styles and in terms of uniformity of uniforms, if you like, within both the Croat and the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn, if I may just for a minute, to the meeting that you described with General Petkovic and Colonel Blaskic. I believe that you said it was on April the 21st of 1993.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you observed Brigadier General Petkovic giving Colonel Blaskic a good dressing down?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would that be too harsh a way to put it or would you phrase it any other way?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I mean he was certainly talking to him in short, sharp words of one syllable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You could certainly appreciate Brigadier General Petkovic's anger if all of the Croat forces found themselves on that day surrounded by Muslim forces and essentially back on their heels in Colonel Blaskic's area of responsibility, could you not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see General Petkovic's face when this exchange was going on?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I could, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you see Colonel Blaskic's face?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself don't know what was said, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your interpreter, I believe, was a nervous type of an individual, you've previously testified in other cases.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was it that he told you that this exchange had consisted of?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There were two aspects to it. The first was his reaction to what he had heard, which had frightened and shocked him, and the second was that he believed that what he had heard could endanger his life and was visibly frightened and shaken. When I then asked him what on Earth he had heard that had caused him to react like this, he then started explaining that essentially General Petkovic had been asking Colonel Blaskic about things being controlled, things not being in the open, things being in the open, and I didn't fully understand at that point what it was about, thought it was largely to do with the defeat of the Croats, albeit they had been together quite a while by this stage and it seemed an odd time to berate him, and that, in itself, didn't appear to make sense as to why my interpreter was so terrified about what he had heard. It was later that the full implications for what he had heard actually sort of became clearer. You would have to understand that as a member of the Muslim community in Central Bosnia, he already knew about certain things we had only heard as specific rumours, i.e., the rumours of massacres which we had heard, and you yourself mentioned some alleged by the HVO earlier, and they were right throughout the whole of Central Bosnia. We were dealing with allegations of massacres north of Tuzla and Srebrenica at the time, and so we had learned not to overreact to the rumours of massacres, and I was not necessarily -- I didn't necessarily have empathy at the time with what my interpreter was trying to explain to me. I hope that puts it in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it does. Thank you. Did you actually look at any milinfosums that immediately preceded your arrival in Central Bosnia to bring yourself up to speed with the recent history of what had been going on?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to show you one milinfosum, number 90, from January 29th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D58/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the liaison officer for Busovaca was at this time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I think it was Captain Martin Foregrave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall reading this particular milinfosum as you were researching recent events in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I read every milinfosum from the day the battalion deployed until I arrived, and I can't recollect a single one of them in isolation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony about mutilations of bodies and things of that variety. Were you aware that there were any mutilations associated with this incident, where supposedly BiH extremists had massacred 12 old people and had arrested a further 30?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I do have a recollection of the murder or massacre of some Croat people by Muslims before my arrival, and I do remember accounts of mutilation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Zvonko Rajic's heart had been cut out of his body after he had been shot to death with about a dozen bullets?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember the detail of the mutilation. It wouldn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. On the third page, there's a reference to Muslims having been arrested, then released, and then there had been incidents of HVO soldiers and Croats being sniped at, and this had left them with no option but to rearrest the Muslims, according to the HVO commander, Commander Niko Jozinovic. On the question of snipers, sir, was it your experience that snipers were an endemic problem in the area throughout your three months in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On both sides?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. All three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All three sides. Do you remember one of the first meetings that you had was with an enterprising merchant in Novi Travnik or Travnik, I believe, who actually manufactured rifle silencers?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He had manufactured a silencer for a Draganoff sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to show you a picture, if I may -- it was reproduced in Colonel Stewart's book -- of a silencer. It appears to be on a rifle, and I would just like to ask you if you've ever seen something like this in your area of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you just take a look at the reproduction of the photograph on the bottom of this page, did you ever see any large rifle silencers, it looks like, of that type when you were in Central Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That appears to have been put on a regular hunting rifle as opposed to a more sophisticated military assault weapon such as an AK-47 or a Draganoff sniper's rifle?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also said, Colonel Watters, that there had been some sniping around your compound at Nova Bila, I think, in the area of April the 16th to the 18th, and do you remember raising the issue of snipers with the HVO commanders at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What they told you was that you should feel free to shoot those people if you could find them; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no doubt, indeed, sir, that the Muslim forces in Stari Vitez were regularly and successfully sniping at Croat positions, is there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, there's no doubt about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe that two Croat soldiers who were participating in the peace negotiations that you brokered on April the 16th were actually shot while they were under the escort of your soldiers. Is that correct? ^^rs

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those were Mr. Marko Prskalo and Mr. Zoran Pilovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct. They were shot just outside the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They were two of the HVO negotiators that were under your protection; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's extremely difficult to tell where a sniper firing at you is actually firing from?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It is difficult, yes. We try and train ourselves to be able to do it. It's impossible if they're using a silencer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And in fact, when you first went to Central Bosnia and the incident I've just described, you actually had a demonstration of the effectiveness of a silenced sniper's rifle up to ranges of up to 200 metres; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You couldn't tell where the shot was coming from at that range, could you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Not from a silenced weapon, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Towards the end of your testimony in chief, Colonel Watters, I believe that you expressed your views about the strategic importance and significance of the main supply routes, the MSRs, running through your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree that, from a military perspective, it was extremely important -- indeed, crucial -- to have those MSRs under effective control?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The protection of those MSRs, the protection of supply routes by which your forces could be reinforced or could reinforce, was a legitimate and important military objective, in your view, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, I believe that you've previously testified, and I think that this was an extremely terse and accurate way to put it, quote: "The man that controls the valleys or the man that controls the routes controls the country."

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's still your view, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that a majority of the fighting that occurred both before the April hostilities and actually during April of 1993 was devoted to efforts to secure these strategically vital main supply routes in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was certainly a major factor. I think there were requirements for taking ground and taking villages, certainly within the Serb agenda. But when one analysed the final front lines of the Serbian positions, as well as their territorial gains, it enabled them to control the main routes that then existed in and out of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And turning -- just narrowing the focus to the Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak area, you would agree that both the Croat side and the Muslim side viewed the control of those main supply routes as an absolutely critical, indeed, overriding, military objective?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, the securing of those main supply routes was a principal objective behind the Muslim counteroffensive or the Muslim offensive, if you like, on April the 18th, 19th, and 20th, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: It was -- I'm not quite sure what their end-state objective was. At one point I was very concerned that their end-state objective was the destruction of Busovaca and Vitez. I had a conversation with General Halilovic to that -- along those lines. The point at which they halted their advance, prior to any final assaults on to Vitez and Busovaca, had severed all the main routes, as I explained, and essentially cut off each of the HVO units and Croatian communities and had essentially isolated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that the Muslim forces' offensive on April the 18th, 19th, and 20th, was incredibly successful?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The forces attacking Croat positions were successful in recapturing basically all of the main choke points, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For example, the Muslim forces took control of the Kaonik junction?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And controlled it until the forces pulled back; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To the north and east of Vitez is a fairly mountainous or hilly area; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Muslim counteroffensive swept down the spinal road that leads from Zenica to Dubravica and then on to Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, as I showed on the map, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Muslim forces, as they were pursuing that military objective, took control of the high ground, as you would expect them to do, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That enabled them to be in a position to shoot down at the Croat forces or whoever happened to be at a lower elevation; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just before the conflict broke out, your testimony, I believe, was that Mr. Mate Boban made a visit to Travnik in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who told you he actually made that visit?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: UNHCR, and our interpreters who lived in Travnik, and the BiH in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You did understand, and I think that there isn't any dispute about this, that he was actually the central political figure in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it was your testimony, I believe, to the Prosecution's investigators two years ago, if they wanted indicators, that things started to go drastically wrong after Mr. Boban's visit to Travnik on April the 8th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony -- I think you briefly touched upon the kidnapping incident involving commander Zivko Totic in Zenica on the evening of April the 15th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was one day before all of the fighting erupted in the Lasva Valley, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see on the television any programmes that depicted the condition in which Commander Totic's bodyguards were left after the kidnapping incident?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't believe I did. I had it described to me that they had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that they had actually been executed?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I mean, "executed," to me, would mean that somebody was sort of stood up with their hands tied behind their back and shot at close quarters. I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that the bodyguards had been wounded in a hail of gunfire and then shot to death by being shot in the head?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I was aware -- I was only aware they had been killed. There had been quite a fierce firefight, and they'd been killed, and the commander hadn't, and had been abducted. I can remember thinking it was a rather strange scenario, at the time, that he would survive and everyone else would die, but that's what had happened, and sometimes life's like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember reports to the effect that it was the 7th Muslim Brigade, or detachments within the 7th Muslim Brigade, that was responsible for that incident?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So-called Mujahedin; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: No, the 7th Brigade weren't Mujahedins. The Mujahedin were a generic term. The 7th Brigade contained soldiers who considered themselves to be Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you also hear reports to the effect that it was the 7th Muslim Brigade that was responsible for kidnapping four other HVO officers the evening before, in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: There was an incident where some -- an escort party went from Novi Travnik to Gornji Vakuf, and I believe they were abducted. I can't remember the exact details of it. They were HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, and abducted by the 7th Muslim Brigade, as far as you were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: That was the information we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it also fair to say that the information you were given concerning the massacre at Dusina was the work of the 7th Muslim Brigade too?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I understand that is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then following Ahmici, there was another massacre, at Miletici, I believe, on the 24th of April, where five young men were tortured and beheaded; was it your understanding that that was the work of the 7th Muslim Brigade as well?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't recollect that incident.
